agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Building Equitable African Partnerships
descriptions: The project aims to establish African-led equitable partnerships focusing on gender, conflict, and creative economies. Building on ten years of previous work in East and Southern Africa, it employs decolonial methodologies and participatory methods. The initiative spans Kenya, South Africa, Mozambique, Namibia, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Uganda, Ethiopia, Sudan, Rwanda, and Lesotho, engaging local communities, activists, grassroots organizations, and stakeholders for broad-based participation and impact. Key themes include digital humanities and the creative economy, women and girls, and conflict/post-conflict humanitarian protection and modern slavery. The project acknowledges the digital divide while promoting inclusivity, primarily focusing on the creative economy. It emphasizes gender equality, addressing challenges faced by women and girls in conflict settings, and explores initiatives to combat modern slavery and promote peacebuilding. The methodology involves comprehensive stakeholder and rights holders identification and engagement, using open calls and mapping to include disadvantaged groups and historically disadvantaged universities. Standards for decolonization ensure equitable management, ethics, data sovereignty, and dissemination. Risk mitigation addresses potential exploitation, inter-group dynamics, and controversial topics through active listening and transparency. The project is divided into four phases: workshop preparation (July - October 2024), two-day workshops (October-November 2024), co-producing outputs (December 2024 - March 2025), and ongoing meetings for future actions (April and May 2025). Gender equality is central, ensuring equal opportunities for participation, leadership, and decision-making. Targeted outreach and a gender-sensitive budget facilitate the involvement of women and underrepresented genders. The project promotes gender equality, reducing discrimination, and fostering solidarity among women. A comprehensive risk assessment and monitoring mechanisms address potential negative impacts on gender equality. The project aims to stimulate innovation, build local capacities, empower marginalized groups, and create sustainable impacts. By enhancing gender equality and fostering relationships between policymakers, decision-makers, civil society, and government officials, it contributes to Sustainable Development Goals like gender equality, decent work and economic growth, and partnerships for the goals.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Detection, Occurrence and Decontamination Strategies for Soluble Toxigenic Fungi and Mycotoxins in Drinking Water Sources in Central and West Africa.
descriptions:
This project will enhance Central and West African capacity for detecting and removing fungal contaminants, ensuring safer drinking water for these communities. We will use our established Network to collect water samples across the region to (i) analyse them for fungi and their toxic compounds, and (ii) develop better detection and decontamination methods for these contaminants.
Fungal contamination in drinking water is gaining global attention and is a key concern within our Network. Toxigenic fungi and mycotoxins, toxic compounds produced by fungi, are well-documented in food, but there are limited data on their prevalence in water. With high demand for clean drinking and agricultural waters, there is a pressing need to investigate toxigenic fungi and mycotoxins in water across Central and West Africa.
This project focuses on fungi identified by experts within the Network including Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Penicillium, and their mycotoxins: aflatoxins, fumonisins, and ochratoxins. We will identify/quantify these using standard methods in the Network and benchmark improvements using advanced techniques such as NMR and electrochemical sensing via UK collaborators. We will develop technical capacity in the region, and new porous materials for more efficient detection and removal of these contaminants from drinking water.
Knowledge gained will target scientists in water quality and materials development, water treatment and distribution professionals, and policymakers, to improve policy and practice. We will conduct workshops and networking activities to build on our successful Network model, including sending researchers and materials to the UK to foster future collaborations and maximize knowledge transfer and training.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Hydro-g  -  Integrating Low-Cost Microgravity Technology into Groundwater Resources Management in sub-Saharan Africa
descriptions:
Across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), approx. 75% of the population depend solely on groundwater for water supplies. Developing sustainable groundwater supplies in SSA is key to communities’ resilience, health & well-being and economic development. However, poorly managed over-exploitation of groundwater is causing degradation of crucial resources and leads to the urgent need for better groundwater monitoring.  Furthermore, the increasingly erratic nature of rainfall patterns disrupts productivity of rain-fed agriculture, contributes to floods and droughts, and stalls economic growth. 
A key strategy to increase the resilience of water supplies is Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR), a water management option that provides a means of intentionally recharging and storing water underground for subsequent recovery and beneficial use. MAR provides an important buffer against the impacts of climate variability.  However, the vast majority of African countries have not implemented MAR.  Successful MAR schemes require a robust assessment of aquifer storage properties and ongoing monitoring of subsurface water storage at the catchment scale. But traditional aquifer testing and groundwater monitoring requires expensive borehole networks which are cost-prohibitive for many countries in SSA.  
The programme will jointly test and benchmark the integration of the new low-cost microgravity sensor technology for water resources management and in particular for MAR schemes with regional stakeholders from the water sector and communities in Burkina Faso, Kenya and South Africa. In doing so, improved resources management using the new low-cost sensor will contribute to building resilience and alleviating poverty in these countries and provide a template for other countries across SSA.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Promoting Just Transitions: The African Transitional Justice Research Network
descriptions: Since the African Transitional Justice Research Network's establishment in 2022, the fragility of the rule of law in Africa has become an increasing concern, emphasizing the importance of our work. Violent conflicts have erupted in Sudan, while ongoing conflicts continue in the DRC, Mozambique, and Ethiopia. Over nine military coups have occurred, and authoritarianism is spreading. Protests against poor governance and corruption, such as those in Kenya, have faced state violence. Although the African Union's adoption of the Transitional Justice Policy (AUTJP) in 2019 appeared to offer a commitment towards the promotion of peace and justice on the continent, its impact has been limited. Given the ongoing challenges to democracy on the continent, stronger collaboration between transitional justice scholars, practitioners, and policymakers to leverage the AUTJP is thus crucial. Our nascent network has continued to collaborate and we have identified a number of priority areas to address African-specific justice needs, including combating widespread gender-based crimes, promoting effective ways of addressing past atrocities, and using the AUTJP to prevent democratic backsliding. We are really excited for this opportunity to expand our already vibrant network of scholars and practitioners as we endeavour to better support human rights defenders across the continent. By identifying successful justice interventions and lessons learned from those within the network, we shall develop targeted, policy-relevant, and African-centered research to strengthen the rule of law and advance the AUTJP's goals of transformative justice. Underpinning our project is a commitment to tackling global challenges through providing impactful research and innovation.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Plant Protein Plus Network UK-SE Asia (3PUKSEA): Multi-disciplinary collaboration for plant protein research and innovation network between the UK and
descriptions:
Food choices impact human and planetary health and therefore transitioning diets to more sustainable sources of protein is crucial. The plant-based protein (PBP) market is growing (estimated US$13.27 billion in 2022) but currently much dependent on imported soyabean causing food-miles and driving deforestation. A major challenge for diversification of the current PBP portfolio are the inability of alternative PBPs to compete with soyabean on price and the concentration of technical investment. This proposal will strengthen the already formed UK-Vietnam network to exploit further opportunities for PBP and rice proteins from 25-35% of waste/side-streams generated in 47 Mt rice production in Vietnam.
The overarching goal is to drive research and networking activities to understand the plausible rice protein value chain and the untapped market opportunity in Vietnam which should culminate into the UK-SE Asia plant protein innovation network to unlock co-benefits of sustainable protein shift and upcycling opportunity. The proposal consists of accelerating network activities including stakeholder engagement and promoting UK-Vietnam research partnership on sustainable protein technologies which would help SE Asia to develop affordable PBP thereby propagating further trade opportunities for the UK. 
The network activities entail organising various research seminars, business innovation events and community engagement workshops to co-create valuable insights on the emerging market landscape of PBP, including socio-economic viability in SE Asia which will help us to perform detailed economic assessment of rice protein value chain and upcycling opportunities. The proposed research will deliver enduring climate-smart innovation by developing transformative technology for re-utilisation of protein-rich focal crops.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Validation of root diameter as a key root trait for stress resilience.
descriptions:
Rice- the primary food crop in Asia/Africa is produced across six continents and is the staple food for ~3 billion people. With increasing population, Global Food Security is one of the major challenges facing world agriculture(1).   This is against the backdrop of global warming and climate unpredictability.  Crop production is especially vulnerable to extremes of environmental stress (drought/heat) leading to significant losses in yield and quality.  To meet the future food demand, there is an urgent need to develop diverse, climate-ready and resilient agricultural systems(1). 
Root traits determine the plant’s capacity to capture nutrients and water and therefore directly influence crop productivity.  This grant builds on from the corresponding networking grant GCRFNGR5\1102. Dr Henry (lead applicant) recently showed that nodal root diameter correlated positively with improved yield under drought stress(2,3).  Interestingly, changes in root diameter have also been correlated with salt(4) and compaction(5) stresses.  Plus, CoI team has observed that primary root diameter is affected under high temperature stress.
This  grant proposal will test the heat tolerance/resilience of lines already selected for drought resilience by the lead applicant.  They will also be subject to detailed root architectural and anatomical studies using X-Ray CT and Laser Ablation tomography.  This programme combines innovative multi-disciplinary approaches to investigate heat/drought tolerance in rice and is likely to provide novel genes for translation into a crop breeding programme. 
1. Bailey-Serres et al2019, Nature 575,109-118.
2. Liao et al,2022,Plant Cell Environ,45:854-870.
3. Siangliw et al,2022,Front Plant Sci13:1008954.
4.Huang et al 2022,PNAS(USA),119,e2201072119. 
5.Huang et al,2021,Int Mol Sci22,10892.

descriptions:

At the heart of the UN Convention on the Rights- of- the Child (2), is the mandate to promote psychological recovery and social reintegration of children affected by armed-conflict. Yet, 468 million or more than 1-in-6 children worldwide live in armed-conflict contexts. Africa remains a region with the highest number of children living in conflict-zones –around 183 million (3)
GCRF networking research identified that children and young-people aged 6-16, affected by Boko-Haram attacks require urgent mental-health support for successful reintegration into school and society, and that Indigenous art methods (I AM) show significant promise in helping children navigate and manage experiences relating to the crisis and should be further tested, adapted, and scaled. 
This grant will bring together an interdisciplinary network of local art-based organisations, mental-health specialists, grassroots NGOs, art-therapists, psychosociologists and researchers in Niger, Chad and UK- to co-design and implement I AM workshops, aimed at developing educational capacity for promoting recovery and reintegration of children affected by the crisis in Niger and Chad.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Mapping Health PPPs in Brazil: key actors and shifts in public provision
descriptions:
Health Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) are advocated by governments and development actors as a means of
bringing financial resources and skills to deteriorating public healthcare services. However, although PPPs bring
much needed resources in the short-term, the long-term effects of these contracts on the health system as a
whole raise some concerns. There is evidence of high contract costs, regulatory challenges and the risks of PPPs
for health inequalities. For example, PPPs can divert public health budgets away from primary and secondary
care and studies reveal that PPP hospitals sometimes exclude users requiring more costly treatments.
Despite these concerns, Brazil, which has one of the largest public health systems in the world, has seen a rapid
expansion of health PPPs. Brazil’s first health PPP contract was signed in 2010 to construct a hospital in Bahia
but to date this remains under-researched. In 2022 there were 118 health PPPs with more planned after a
change in the PPP law in 2023. Yet there is a lack of publicly accessible knowledge and understanding of this
process. Moreover, anecdotal evidence highlights the importance of PPP policy diffusion from the UK to Brazil
despite the acknowledged failure of the UK Private Finance Initiative in healthcare. Thus, our project has three
objectives: to comprehensively map all of the health PPPs, identifying the key actors and their strategies behind
each contract; to create a publicly accessible database of Brazilian health PPPs to monitor their impact; to
understand the role of UK support in the PPP expansion.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Responding to calls from the NTD Affected Voices
descriptions:
Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are a group of 21 mostly communicable diseases affecting over 1.7 billion people. These diseases debilitate, disfigure and can be fatal. They create and lock people into vicious cycles of poverty and cost developing nations billions of dollars annually.
 As indicated in the 2024 World Health Organization (WHO) NTD report, the current global and national efforts on NTD control  are neglecting health service delivery to people living with NTD-related disease, disability and disfigurement.  In our GCFR Network grant we brought together NTD researchers, social scientists, the NGO sector, policy makers, primary health practitioners, community health workers, and people with lived experiences  (affected voices) across the age range and gender spectrum  from Tanzania, Sudan and Zimbabwe, to develop a roadmap for collective action in addressing the health inequalities and health service deficiencies faced by the affected voices. This follow-on project aims to deliver the following directives from this consultative  process:
1.Mainstream and evaluate quantification of chronic NTD burden in health and elimination metrics.
2.Developing an algorithm for the detection of invisible chronic morbidities for their early detection and timely management.
3.Progress the development of  NTD preventative and diagnostic tools
4.Strengthening capacity of primary healthcare to manage NTD chronic morbidities while promoting/capacitating the affected on self care and management of morbidities in normal and insecurity/ internal displacement communities. 
5.Establishing national platforms for amplifying the voices of the NTD affected for accelerated access to curative/rehabilitative interventions and to address NTD-related stigma/discrimination

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: RURAL_SURG: Developing community strategies to strengthen access to surgical care in rural Africa
descriptions:
Millions of people worldwide get sick or die from conditions that are treatable by surgery, the majority of whom live in Africa. In our AfroSurg network we found that people living in rural areas are less likely than those in cities to get surgical care when needed; novel solutions are needed to reach those that need treatment. Indigenous practitioners and community health workers are members of rural communities who can potentially sensitise persons with surgical conditions about their disease and refer them into formal medical care. We propose to co-create strategies with these groups in AfroSurg countries, South Africa, Malawi, and Zambia, to improve access to surgical care for rural persons.
We will build surgical community networks of stakeholders to discover reasons for delays to care, create screening tools and referral mechanisms, and develop trainings to address these issues. Our proposal is important because we will work directly with the community and front-line health workers to develop solutions together.  Direct beneficiaries of improved access to surgical care will be communities, patients, healthcare providers, and policymakers in these countries. 
The proposal has the potential to improve health and well-being and reduce inequality between rural and urban communities leading to more productive and resilient societies. If solutions are judged to be transferable, we plan to assess how to scale-up amongst the rest of the AfroSurg network - which now spans 16 countries in Southern Africa - and maximise impact for patients, communities, and countries.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: CANARIES II: FLIGHT - Framework for Live Animal Market Investigations and Guidelines Harmonization and Techniques in Africa and Asia
descriptions:
Since the establishment of CANARIES through GCRF in 2019, the biosecurity risk of live-animal markets (LAMs) has become even more evident through the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 and continued circulation of avian influenza. Despite the resulting this global focus, LAMs continue to pose a risk to global health. LAMs are of economic and cultural importance, thus forcing their closure is not appropriate, potentially leading to black-markets.  
In this project, CANARIES will strengthen and expand upon its existing network to further understand the risks associated with LAMs. To do so, we will convene a networking meeting which will simultaneously reinvigorate the network and draw on the collective expertise of CANARIES to develop a framework that will enable us to evaluate risks associated with LAMs. The framework will be trialled in selected countries in Asia and Africa. Following further optimisation (if required) and capacity building developed during a follow-up meeting, the framework will be made available to an expanded network of stakeholders for global application. Using a standardised data collection tool developed by international researchers with real-world experience, we will be able to compare and evaluate biosecurity risks associated with LAMs in diverse settings. Our work will lead to the identification of interventions that can be implemented through the lens of cultural and economic sustainability, thus improving health outcomes of LAM users while maintaining the social fabric of local communities. This work will positively impact on various sustainable development goals.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Indonesia-UK network on vector-borne disease modelling for public health policy
descriptions:
Vector-borne diseases, such as dengue and chikungunya, are responsible for devastating consequences. The causal viruses often spread in low- and middle-income countries, with Aedes moquitoes (which spread many vector-borne diseases) being particularly prevalent in tropical regions. Global disease prevalence has been increasing in recent decades, including outbreaks in previously unaffected locations. Factors such as urbanization, increased travel, and climate change are contributing to the growing prevalence of these diseases, highlighting the need for ongoing research and monitoring to manage and predict outbreaks effectively.
This project involves the development of an Indonesia-UK vector-borne disease modelling network, with a focus on capacity building. Indonesia is a country that experiences frequent outbreaks of vector-borne disease, and the UK is a country that is expected to experience outbreaks in the coming decades. As such, researchers in the UK will benefit from the experience of Indonesian researchers at living with and managing vector-borne disease, and researchers in Indonesia will benefit from the infectious disease modelling expertise in the UK. 
Specific topics for joint study include: i) Identifying patterns of virus transmission in different regions in Indonesia; ii) Examining the impact of different virus strains; iii) Modelling the interaction between environmental factors and mosquito population dynamics; and iv) Outbreak forecasting. Discussions will generate insights for disease control in Indonesia and demonstrate general principles for preventing disease in the UK. This initiative will facilitate knowledge exchange between UK and Indonesia experts, and provide learning opportunities for students in both countries.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: MUXNET - Multisensory XR-based Telesurgery
descriptions: MUXNET explores how the innovative combination of  telesurgery with multisensory XR and telecommunication technologies can be used to complement medical workers’ skills and what policy recommendations should be adopted within the European medical sector. To this end, the proposed project will explore a novel training framework that involves  enabling technologies centered on multisensory extended reality (XR) and telecommunications in the context of telesurgery. Hence, in this context, MUXNET  will not only incorporate a novel 9 degrees of freedom (9-DoF) haptic glove but also additionally explore the effectiveness of the olfactory modality in XR by harnessing the power of aromas such as rosemary and lavender to benefit cognitive processing, and consequently, enhance learning and training. Using tactile and visual senses to experience first-hand activities in a distant setting is a relatively new field, but the addition of olfactory stimuli not just to heighten the learning experience of medical professionals, but also to enhance the immersive nature of telesurgery training makes the project a total game changer in the area of multisensory XR. The training outcomes of using such innovative technologies will thus be explored with a view to ensuring their sustainable and wide adoption in the medical sector and defining policies regarding Digital Citizens 2.0. Accordingly, MUXNET adopts an approach whereby training is formulated as a result of experiences gained exploring novel applications of existing cutting-edge technologies in hitherto unexplored scenarios in the medical sector. In so doing, MUXNET enables collaboration, resource sharing, and community building between UK and Turkey.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Unravelling the Role of the Microbiome in Mental Health Disorders in Africa
descriptions: Mental health disorders are a growing concern across the world, especially in Africa, where limited resources make it difficult to provide adequate care. Interestingly, recent research suggests that the microbes living in our gut (known as the gut microbiome) may play an important role in mental health, potentially affecting mood, anxiety, and depression. Several studies have been done to investigate the relationship between mental health and the gut microbiome, but the majority of these studies have been done in Asian and European populations. Therefore, little is known about how these microbes influence mental health in African populations. Our project aims to bring together experts from Africa and the UK to explore the connection between the microbiome and mental health in Africa. Through a series of virtual meetings and an in-person workshop, we will discuss existing research and identify the most important challenges that need to be addressed. We are particularly excited about this work because it could lead to new ways of improving mental health by targeting the gut microbiome, which could provide affordable and accessible treatments. By creating a network of experts across different fields, we hope to build long-lasting collaborations that will improve mental health research in Africa. The potential impact of this work is significant: better understanding how gut microbes affect mental health could lead to new strategies for preventing and treating mental illnesses. These findings could benefit millions of people, improving mental health care and overall well-being in Africa and beyond.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: POWER: A POpulation Health WEaRables Network in Low- and Middle-income Countries.
descriptions: Non-communicable diseases (NCD), including cancer and heart disease, account for seven out of ten deaths globally, the majority of which occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Better understanding of risk factors for these diseases, which include lifestyle behaviours such as insufficient physical activity, is crucial to reversing this trend. The availability of wearable devices that can measure physical behaviours (eg walking, sitting) and environmental factors (eg air quality, temperature) has grown significantly in recent years. These devices are transforming our understanding of how lifestyle behaviours, and the contexts in which they take place, influence NCD-related risk and deaths. This is because they provide more accurate and detailed information about these factors than self-report questionnaires. Use of these devices in research, however, has been almost exclusively in high-income countries. We know little about the duration and location of physical behaviours measured by wearables in LMICs, for example. This is important because the types of behaviours undertaken and the environments in which they take place varies greatly between countries; this can result in differing associations with health and the need for tailored approaches to changing unhealthy behaviour patterns. The aim of this project is to build a network of researchers to support greater use of wearables to measure physical behaviours and environmental factors in LMICs. We will identify the interests and priorities of network members, barriers and enablers to the use of wearable devices in different settings, and establish new collaborations to support wider use of wearables in LMIC-based projects.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Spatial brain-computer interface technologies for recovery after neurosurgery and neurotrauma.
descriptions:
Every year, traumatic injury to the brain and spinal cord (neurotrauma) affects almost 100 million people world-wide and costs the global economy £350 billion. This project aims to develop brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies that use immersive three-dimensional and artificial intelligence (AI) systems that can assist recovery in patients after neurosurgery and neurotrauma. Our approach is non-invasive and focuses on improving the nervous system’s natural ability to restore function after injury. By creating an interdisciplinary collaboration between Malaysian and UK research teams, we will leverage expertise in neuroscience, neurosurgery, neurorehabilitation, engineering, and computer science to advance this innovative technology.
The network will focus on transferring knowledge, skills, and technical capabilities in global BCI development, fostering partnerships that can conduct high-impact research. The goal is to develop a prototype that could be affordable and applicable to global populations, which could significantly improve recovery outcomes in patients. This project addresses the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3—Good Health and Well-being—by targeting neurorehabilitation, a crucial healthcare challenge globally, particularly in lower-income settings where access to rehabilitation expertise and technology is often lacking.
Through workshops, collaborative meetings, and training, this network will build capacity, develop talent, and pave the way for future large-scale funding opportunities. By the end of the grant, we aim to establish a sustainable partnership that fosters the ongoing exchange of skills and innovation between Malaysia and the UK.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Coastal Land Loss: Northern Java Indonesia-UK Hub
descriptions:
The project aims to create the collaborative hub “CLINcH - Coastal Land loss: INdonesia-UK Hub”, bringing together experts focused on enhancing infrastructure and resilience in case of coastal land loss. The hub will concentrate its research on the estuary area of the Citarum River along the Northern Java coastline, specifically in the Bekasi District of West Java Province. This region has witnessed significant land loss, posing severe risks to both communities and coastal ecosystems. Over the past two decades, the shoreline in Muara Gembong has retreated at a rate of up to 200 m/year, leading to coastal inundation and jeopardizing various infrastructure systems. This phenomenon has been intensified by environmental changes, such as mangrove removal, and unregulated activities along the Citarum River, like waste disposal. These factors, coupled with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather events and sea level rise, have exacerbated the situation.
CLINCH will focus on: 1. Understanding coastal land loss; 2. Assessing resulting flood risk and vulnerability of infrastructure systems and social economy of local community; 3. Evaluating the capacities/vulnerabilities of the region. 4. Facilitating the exchange of knowledge and best practices between the hub and various stakeholders.
The hub will serve as a centre of expertise, aiding in the development of improved management plans and investment strategies. This will not only benefit stakeholders in Indonesia and the UK, but also those in other countries facing similar challenges. The project will improve community awareness about coastal land loss and the importance of wetlands

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: AI-driven approaches to climate-resilient malaria control
descriptions:
Malaria remains one of the most significant public health challenges in Africa, accounting for 94% of cases and 95% of deaths globally in 2022 (WHO 2023). Climate change is expected to exacerbate this problem by altering mosquito behavior and malaria transmission patterns. Initiatives such as the rollout of malaria vaccines and public health campaigns like "Zero Palu" in countries like Benin have made notable progress in reducing malaria cases. However, despite these efforts, malaria transmission remains unpredictable due to the increasingly variable weather patterns caused by climate change.
Our project, AI-CLIMAL, aims to harness the power of AI to develop innovative, climate-resilient solutions for malaria control. By establishing a collaborative network of researchers and stakeholders from the UK and sub-Saharan Africa, we will create AI tools that analyze climate, mosquito population, and health data. Through a series of workshops and virtual seminars, our project will facilitate knowledge exchange; helping experts understand how AI can enhance current malaria prevention efforts, including vaccine programs, and target interventions more effectively; and developing research and development projects for next steps. 
Ultimately, AI-CLIMAL seeks to combine cutting-edge technology with traditional public health strategies, offering a comprehensive approach to malaria control. This approach will improve the accuracy of malaria outbreak predictions, empowering public health authorities to take proactive, preemptive actions in high-risk areas. The long-term goal of the project is to save lives, reduce the burden of malaria on affected communities, and build resilience against the health impacts of climate change.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Recent advances and Challenges in Antimicrobial Resistance: Threat from the pink corner
descriptions: The alarming rise in the emergence of antimicrobial resistance and its impact on the global health is still challenging. This global health crisis threatens the medical advancements and Public Health that have been achieved in the past century. This will ultimately lead to resurgence of previously manageable infectious diseases and results in devastating cost on human society due to increased debilitating and life-threatening infections in frequency and scope. Acinetobacter baumannii is a critical priority pathogen listed by the World Health Organisation. Monitoring of antimicrobial resistance through surveillance approaches has always been a historical problem. This topic is particularly important in low- and middle-income countries like Egypt, where resources for investigating mechanisms of AMR, surveillance and monitoring, diagnosis and treatment are limited.  Our work is significant and exciting because it has the potential to change the way we approach infectious diseases particularly in low-middle income countries.  Significant strides have been made in understanding antimicrobial resistance mechanisms but focus also needs to be on improving diagnostic tools and finding viable therapeutic options as vaccines, bacteriophages as a novel therapy to combat antimicrobial resistance which is why this work has been proposed. With new technologies, novel therapies and interdisciplinary collaborations, there is real hope for developing innovative treatments and prevention strategies. The potential impact of this research is vast; it has economic implications, fewer deaths, decreased healthcare costs and decreased hospitalisation.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Southern Africa-UK Network on Child Health and Air Pollution
descriptions:
Our grant proposal aims to establish a robust network led by our partnership team in Southern Africa and the UK, with a central focus on air pollution and child health. This research area was chosen because whilst air pollution affects everyone, children and adolescents are especially susceptible as their bodies, organs and immune systems are still developing. Whilst there have been excellent systematic reviews on the topic, there has been no mapping reviews which span the full health impacts for children across the full suite of air pollutants. 
Our proposal seeks to develop a network of academics and policy makers interested understanding the current evidence base, and subsequently, developing research proposals for priority questions which will address key gaps in the field. This collaboration will benefit all those in the research network and will also spearhead further research in the field.
We will prioritise the importance of capacity building among early career researchers, whereby less experienced colleagues will be partnered with more established network members to identify future research opportunities. We are also committed to understanding what equitable research between Global North and Global South partners looks like and will co-develop guidelines to aid future researchers.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Networking and research enrichment on applying community-based participatory research for healthy ageing in older people (CPR4Health): Bridging gaps a
descriptions: Our Malaysian research in older people and exercise stemmed from studies in sarcopenia, an age-related muscle mass and strength loss disease. We realized that a plethora of beneficial evidence on exercise and nutrition are in journals, but rarely used by older people that would benefit from it the most. Currently, we are testing a system called ENHance-M – Evidence-, Needs-based Healthy ageing Services for older Malaysian adults. ENHance-M uses an older-adult, user-friendly smartphone application that functions like an Uber/Grab app. Instead of calling for rides/food delivery, it calls for trained health service providers (HSPs) for personalized home-based consultations. These HSPs are health science graduates, up-skilled via our ENHance-M online micro-credential courses to ensure standardized quality care. ENHance-M’s potential is multifold – from providing older people with accessible and reliable health services at home, to job opportunities for health graduates in their hometown using the gig work model. Yet, we lack insight if ENHance-M is something that Malaysian older adults would embrace. Thus, we intend to learn, apply and network around community-based participatory research (CPR) to establish older adults and HSPs thoughts/feelings about and consequences of ENHance-M. We would also like to extend CPR practices to other researchers in older people in Malaysia and consequently, create a Malay language training module from the experience. Our network will bring experienced CPR academics from University of Dundee together with HSPs, policy makers and related non-governmental organizations to ensure ENHance-M and other community-related research works for older people to bring positive impact and change.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: International Survey of Childbirth-Related Trauma (INTERSECT) Africa

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Health Systems Network  for Non-Communicable Diseases in the Horn of Africa
descriptions: The prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is increasing globally, and particularly in low-and-medium-income countries (LMICs) where it has been estimated that about 70% of all NCD cases will reside by 2045 (1). The case in the horn of Africa (HoA) region (Somaliland/Somalia, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Djibouti) is particularly worse due to poverty, climate change and many system-related challenges (such as lack of skilled workers, poor infrastructure, insufficient health care facilities and lack/inadequacy of policies) (2,3). Our ongoing work within the region indicates that policy makers and researchers are not properly trained to identify health system challenges and to implement effective interventions  for the prevention and management of NCDs (3,4). Where expertise are available, researchers and policy workers work in isolation, making their efforts ineffective.  As part of efforts to strengthen health systems for effective prevention and management of NCDs in the region, we propose the establishment of a network between researchers in the UK and across HoA to facilitate the sharing of best practices, collaboration, mentorship, cross-fertilisation of idea, and, in the future, the establishment of a regional centre for health system research. Funding requested through this application will be used to commence these activities.  We will organise a series of training programmes and idea generation/agenda-setting meetings for researchers, policy makers and community-interest groups in HoA, produce a working-document and launch an online platform for the coordination of the Network's activities.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Strengthening UK-Thai research capacity for AI application to Neglected Infectious Disease
descriptions: Each year, over 1.6 billion people around the globe would be affected by at least one of Neglected Tropical Diseases or NTDs [1]. As a response, WHO developed the NTD road map for 2021-2030 [2] to identify necessary actions to control and eradicate NTDs. Research and innovation are highlighted as fundamental factors to future success, especially potential applications of new technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) and satellite imagery. Specific to leishmaniasis, one of 20 NTDs that is prevalent in tropical areas such as Thailand, the increasing number of asymptomatic cases has been witnessed in this ASEAN country since 1999 [3], mainly among patients with HIV. Recently, a team of local medical experts (led by the Center of Excellence in Vector Biology and Vector Borne Diseases at Chulalongkorn University) have discovered new cases and their associations to sand flies found in rural communities [4-5]. However, those findings are based on the gold standard of parasitological diagnosis that can be tedious and time-consuming [6]. The procedure requires skilled technicians that is a challenge in low-resourced developing countries. To overcome this bottleneck, the proposed project is to develop a roadmap of AI technology exploitation, which is largely missing in the current literature [7]. The network of UK, Thai and other international partners will carry out a pilot study based on existing data and AI techniques to demonstrate actual applications and identify challenges to similar analysis tasks and other NTDs. Publication and dissemination workshops are also included to extend the scope of knowledge sharing.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Brazil-UK network on Speech Sound Disorder
descriptions:
Speech sound disorder (SSD) is the most common condition referred to speech and language therapy services worldwide. Research on population study data carried out by the UK applicant has shown that 3.8% of 8-year-old children have persistent speech sound disorder and they are more likely to have problems with educational achievement, peer relationships and well-being and have a greater risk of self-harm with suicidal intent than other children of their age.
There are over 40 interventions which have been developed for children with speech sound disorder but limited information on which work best. In the UK, we have established a Core Outcome Set (an agreed set of measures to use at the beginning and end of intervention to measure progress in speech) to be used in routine clinical care. This will lead to a large dataset which can then be examined using statistical techniques to determine which intervention works best for different subtypes of speech sound disorder. 
Researchers from the University of Sao Paulo want to develop an adaptation of this Core Outcome Set. A simple translation is not possible because of the differences in Brazilian Portuguese compared to UK English. This network will facilitate the development of a Brazilian version of the Core Outcome Set and a process which can be used to establish other international versions of the tool. Follow-on research funding will be sought to investigate the data from cross-linguistic versions of the tool to address questions of effectiveness of interventions for children with speech sound disorder.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: UK-Indonesia-Malaysia Alliance for Occupational Safety and Health Advancement in Construction (OSH-Advance)
descriptions:
This project aims to improve occupational safety and health (OSH) in the construction sector by establishing a collaborative network between academia, industry, and government in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the UK. Both Malaysia and Indonesia face significant challenges in construction safety, with their construction industries accounting for nearly 30% of workplace fatalities (DOSH, 2024; Lestari et al., 2020). In contrast, the UK has achieved significant improvements in workplace safety over the past five decades, largely due to the introduction of regulations and other interventions. These regulations, combined with proactive measures like enhancing safety culture, comprehensive risk management, and continuous safety training, have contributed to a 90% reduction in workplace fatalities and the creation of safer environments across industries (Reals, 2024). 
 
This project seeks to leverage the UK's extensive experience to assist Malaysia and Indonesia address their own OSH challenges. By fostering knowledge exchange and co-creating tailored solutions and research, the project aims to reduce accidents, strengthen safety culture, and improve OSH practices in both countries' construction industries. 
 
The potential impact is substantial. Enhanced OSH practices will not only improve workplace safety but also promote economic resilience by reducing workplace disruptions, lowering healthcare costs, and improving overall worker welfare. This collaboration could serve as a model for other emerging economies, demonstrating the value of international cooperation in OSH.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Perspectives and Challenges in the Adoption of AI-Based Quality Control in Manufacturing SMEs: A Comparative Study of the UK and South Africa
descriptions:
In 2023, the UK had over 268,175 manufacturing small and medium enterprises (SMEs) (Statsta, 2023), while South Africa had approximately 17,981 (SEDA, 2023). Both industries significantly contribute to economic growth by promoting innovation and providing jobs. However, UK SMEs often benefit from stronger access to modern technology and worldwide export markets, whereas South African SMEs confront obstacles such as weak infrastructure and restricted capital.
Quality control is vital for manufacturing SMEs, assuring consistent product quality, decreasing faults, and saving waste (Alshahrani & Husain, 2024). It promotes consumer satisfaction, strengthens brand reputation, and boosts profitability by boosting efficiency and decreasing expenses. Moreover, it helps SMEs comply with industry regulations more effectively.
Recent research highlights the increasing integration of AI in quality control systems, enabling automation, real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and faster fault identification. AI-driven quality control may minimize human error, enhance efficiency, and improve scalability, making SMEs more competitive globally (Ibrahim et al., 2024).
This study will evaluate the obstacles and potential in adopting AI-based quality control in UK and South African SMEs. It will provide assistance for key stakeholders, including SMEs, policymakers, and AI technology suppliers, to establish effective AI adoption plans, supporting programs like the AI Sector Deal and Industry 4.0. Aligned with UNSDGs, particularly SDG 9 and SDG 8, the project encourages sustainable industrialization and inclusive growth.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Asia-UK Maternal-neonatal Infection and IMmunity Network (AMMUNet)
descriptions:
Infections during pregnancy, childbirth, and the early neonatal period are a major cause of maternal and newborn illness and death, especially in low-resource settings like Nepal. This is highlighted by the total number of 113 maternal deaths, 115 congenital birth defects, and 2,186 perinatal deaths per 100,000 live births, reported in a recent national annual health report. Immunization of pregnant women has the potential to prevent many of these complications, yet there remains a significant data and research gap on the topic. To address this gap, we are running a pilot study at Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital (PMWH) in Kathmandu – the oldest and largest public referral maternity hospital in Nepal, aiming to determine the prevalence of maternal-newborn colonization of Group B Streptococcus (GBS) which is one of the major killers in any healthcare settings. Building on this, we propose to establish the "Asia-UK Maternal-Newborn Infection and Immunity Network (AMMUNet)". 
The network plans to host a three-day residential induction workshop in Kathmandu in early May/June 2025. It will bring together experts from the UK, USA, India and Nepal to strengthen North-South academic partnerships and foster knowledge exchange, with plans to expand ongoing GBS pilot study to additional sites in Nepal and India. The network also aims to fill in the key data gaps in the region to prepare for research and roll out of new maternal vaccines. Together, the network will seek larger grants to support this crucial work, ultimately aiming to improve healthcare for mothers and their newborns.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Co-designing Climate-Resilient Development Pathways: A Framework for Enhancing Inclusive Decision-making across the Food-Water-Land-Ecosystems NeXus i
descriptions: Ethiopia is one of the fastest-growing East African economies with rapid agricultural intensification/transformation and energy production expansion/diversification [1]. Yet, millions of people still live in poverty and without access to basic necessities, e.g., food, water, energy. Ethiopia is also highly vulnerable to climatic shocks (e.g., floods/droughts) and other natural hazards (e.g., landslides/soil erosion) that continuously undermine development efforts and exacerbate poverty levels [2]. In 2024, as of May alone, ~0.6 million people were affected by floods, with 95,000 people displaced, 60,000ha cropland damaged, ~3,000 livestock deaths, and >90 districts with reported cholera outbreaks [3]. These factors present ‘wicked’ challenges for Ethiopia, with cascading and far-reaching repercussions for food production, water resources, land use, and ecosystem conservation/restoration; collectively known as the Food-Water-Land-Ecosystems (FWLE) nexus dilemma; understanding of which is fundamental for achieving at least six of the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals [4]: SDG2 (e.g., sustainable food production); SDG6 (improving water-use efficiency); SDG11 (planned urbanisation); SDG12 (integrated water/land management); SDG13 (data-driven climate policy); SDG15 (biodiversity loss reduction). Previous studies ignore FWLE nexus interactions, resulting in over-/under-estimation of critical climate adaptation needs [5]. Furthermore, Ethiopia’s current climate policies are often siloed and sector-focused, failing to capture the complex FWLE nexus synergies/trade-offs and limiting the ability to develop robust cross-sectoral climate adaptation strategies [6]. This project brings together a diverse group of stakeholders to develop a decision support framework that integrates climate resilience across the FWLE nexus, offering evidence-based guidance for sustainable resources use/management, disaster risk reduction, and long-term development planning in Ethiopia [7].

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: An international and interdisciplinary network for analysing routine HIV/AIDS and cancer registry data in Tanzania
descriptions:
The world is now in the era of “big data”, in both dimensionality, size, and complexity, this includes but not limited to routinely collected health data. The use of routine data significantly contributes to guiding public decisions regarding resource needs and allocation. The data analytical capacity to support management, analysis, and provision of meaningful and relevant interpretations is paramount, but is a bottleneck in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) countries [1,2].
Our interdisciplinary research network will focus on imparting theoretical and practical skills to early career researchers for analysing routinely collected HIV/AIDS and cancer outcomes patient data using deep survival neural networks and advanced statistical methods for longitudinal and time-to-event data. The long-term goal of establishing a strong research network that addresses key questions to improve the key cancer and HIV/AIDS outcomes in Tanzania. 
We build on our previous success with the International Biometric Society (IBS) Tanzania 2022 workshop, “Application of Statistical Learning to Routine Data in Low- and Middle-Income Countries” held at Mwanza Intervention Unit (MITU) in Mwanza and a series of virtual meetings, including the most recent career panel session through the IBS Tanzanian region in September 2024. Based on these events, we observed and identified three major gaps in the field of health research in Tanzania. One is analytical capacity, second is lack of mentorship for early-career researchers and third is lack of recognition of a few (bio)statisticians and data analysts in the country. Our network will bring together key stakeholders on board to work in closing these gaps.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Climate Geopolitics, Critical Minerals Trade, and Sustainable Mining Governance in Indonesia
descriptions:
This interdisciplinary network combines expertise from political scientists, chemists, economists, and international law scholars to offer more holistic solutions to complex mining governance issues.
Our goal is to understand the opportunities and challenges of the evolving mineral resource partnership between the EU and Indonesia, and how this cooperation influences climate adaptation strategies in the mining sector. Clean energy transitions significantly increase demand for critical minerals, and Indonesia accounts for a third of global nickel and tin production. As deepening trading relationships have shifted a large share of emissions from richer to poorer countries, Global South nations are increasingly resisting international decarbonization efforts. While extractive industries like nickel mining generate jobs and growth, they also destroy ecosystems, expose residential communities to health risks, and exacerbate social justice problems as many new mineral developments are located on land held by indigenous and land-dependent people. We will analyse how voters, civil society actors, and decisionmakers weigh minerals trade objectives against development and foreign policy goals. 
Economists and political scientists will collaborate to understand which factors influence public opinion on mining, legal scholars will collaborate with chemists to ensure that laws reflect the latest scientific understanding of mining impacts, and chemists will help social scientists quantify the true costs of pollution. By combining perspectives, each discipline will fill in crucial information that might not emerge within siloed fields of study. It will help develop a common language for discussing mining governance and provide insights on how to design laws that are feasible and enforceable.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Establishing the "South-East Asia Mental Health Consortium" (SEAMHC)
descriptions:
Mental health literacy refers to the knowledge and understanding needed to assess mental health, and recognise mental distress and illness in order to request help and support. In South-East Asia, however, mental health literacy may remain limited due to cultural, social, and structural barriers in conducting mental health research. The "South-East Asia Mental Health Consortium" (SEAMHC), based in Malaysia, seeks to bridge this gap by creating a collaborative network of researchers, educators, healthcare professionals, and policymakers working together to identify best practices and plan public health initiatives to nurture mental health and reduce stigma associated with mental illness and distress, therefore improving access to mental health care for millions of people in Malaysia and neighbouring countries.
This networking grant will support the organisation of the first "SEAMHC Summer School 2025", a 3-day event in Summer 2025, aimed at formally establishing the SEAMHC and discuss future opportunities for collaborative research, knowledge exchange, and capacity-building initiatives. We will invite academics, educators, healthcare professionals, and policymakers from Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, who will contribute and share their expertise. Dr. Hoo Keat Wong (University of Nottingham Malaysia) & Dr. Alessio Bellato (University of Southampton UK) will lead the networking event, which will include a half-day training on evidence synthesis for policymaking, oral and poster presentations, roundtables and workshops.
Establishing the SEAMHC aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 "Good Health and Wellbeing", recognized by the Malaysian government as a critical component for building resilient communities.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: South Africa-UK network of Proteostasis in Diseases
descriptions: The guardians of protein quality control are mainly molecular chaperones that facilitate the correct folding of other proteins to achieve their functional structure. The molecular chaperones mainly the heat shock proteins also assist in their refolding after unfolding events and also facilitate the removal of those proteins unfolded beyond redemption. This process is also known as protein homeostasis or in short as proteostasis. Disturbances in the maintenance of proteostasis result in several plants, human and animal diseases. As such, the number of African scientists and researchers focusing on understanding the role of protein quality control in the development of diseases is increasing. However, there is no coordinated platform to share ideas, protocols and networking across the traditional disciplines. We seek to establish a network of scientists researching on proteostasis towards establishing a chapter of Proteostasis in Africa. This platform will enhance the recruitment and training of young scientists including networking with sister networking platforms in the United States and in the United Kingdom.  We envisage that such a platform will assist to plug the shortage of skills and capacity on understanding the role that these protein quality control processes play in several disease pathophysiology which could be instrumental in setting the stage to enable the African based scientists to answer these questions towards generating solutions to African problems by Africans.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Establishing a roadmap for the advancement of wound pathogen detection and treatment through the utilization of microneedle technology
descriptions:
Chronic wounds, such as ulcers caused by diabetes and sores due to prolonged pressure, are a significant worldwide health problem that impacts millions of people. Effective treatment for chronic wounds is crucial because of the potential for severe consequences, such as infections and amputations.
The long-term objective of our research is to create a novel device based on cutting-edge microneedle technology that rapidly identifies pathogenic germs in wounds and administers drugs. This field of study was selected because of the inefficiency and lack of precision in current wound treatment techniques in general and Egypt in specific. By integrating cutting-edge materials such as quantum dots with microneedles, we anticipate the development of a very effective solution for chronic wounds. This concept of wound care management is highly stimulating since it embodies an innovative approach to an urgent healthcare issue, integrating technology and medicine to enhance patient results.
The potential influence of our research extends beyond individual patients. We aim to provide healthcare practitioners with a dependable instrument for monitoring and treating wounds to alleviate the burden on hospitals and healthcare systems. This can reduce hospitalisation durations, decrease treatment expenses, and improve patient well-being. Our research seeks to establish a foundation for groundbreaking advancements in wound care, which will positively impact society by enhancing general well-being and minimizing difficulties related to long-lasting wounds.
The proposed network will complete the preliminary work (collection of pilot data, future research questions, etc) to achieve the above goal in consultation with key Egyptian and UK partners.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Molecular farming in African biomanufacturing: A UK-Southern Africa partnership for enhancing vaccine production and biosecurity capacity
descriptions:
This project explores how we can use plants to produce vaccines and medicines more quickly, affordably, and flexibly. Molecular farming leverages plants as cell factories to produce essential biologics, such as vaccines and biotherapeutics.
A major challenge Africa faces is its reliance on other regions for vaccines and medicines, which can lead to shortages during health crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Our project, in collaboration with expert partners from the UK, led by Imperial College, focuses on building local capacity in Southern Africa to produce these vaccines and therapies. This will strengthen Africa’s ability to respond rapidly to health emergencies and ensure that supply chains remain robust during crises. By supporting plant-based production, we aim to diversify manufacturing methods, potentially reducing supply chain bottlenecks and improving access to vital treatments.
An exciting aspect of our work is that our network will help identify and prioritize the next pipeline of vaccines and biotherapeutics for clinical development in the region. We will evaluate plant-based production as a potential leapfrogging option alongside other well-established expression systems, such as mammalian or microbial cells. By comparing these systems, we aim to develop decision-support frameworks to determine which production method is best suited for each type of vaccine or therapeutic. Ultimately, this initiative will enable Africa to take a leadership role in vaccine and therapeutic production, working in close partnership with the UK.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Museums and the Ethics of Care: Realising the Potential of Museums for Well-being and Gender Equality
descriptions:
This proposal seeks to develop a network focussed on exploring the entangled role of museum work and care work. In recognising that the Asian museum often foregrounds values around respect for family, place and ancestors (Were 2022), this proposal brings together a new network of academics working in museums, gender and anthropology alongside key practitioners working in the sector to explore museum practice that are infused with ideals of compassion, empathy and healing.
The project’s core ambition is to establish a series of online and face-to-face workshops from which to challenge the way we understand Vietnamese museums by acknowledging their productive nature and their capacity to address societal issues through education, exhibition and research. By framing discussions around the ethics of care, we will discuss ways in which museums act as active agents in addressing social issues in Vietnam around gender identity and aging (Chatterjee & Noble 2013; Morse (2021). A major outcome of the workshops will be the framework for developing a large collaborative grant application to the British Academy.
The network will consist of experts in their fields of anthropology, gender and Asian studies – all of whom have conducted long-term research in sites across Asia – to maximise vitality, success and impact. This project will have impact in Asia as it constructs a framework for understanding the future social role of museums which can also be applied in Europe, following campaigns in the UK such as ‘Museums Matter’ which identifies the museum’s role in civil society strengthening.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Improving outcomes and experiences: the development of a collaborative adolescent maternity care network in Sub-Saharan Africa
descriptions: Adolescent pregnancy is a global concern, with estimates suggesting that 21 million girls aged 15–19 years in LMICs become pregnant, resulting in 12 million births [1]. More concerning is younger adolescents, aged under 15, accounting for approximately 777,000 births. Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has the highest global fertility rate, with 101 births per 1000 adolescents aged 15-19, compared with 12 births per 1000 in HICs [2]. Adolescents are a known vulnerable group, with pregnancy at a young age impacting on lifelong health and wellbeing. Poorer birth outcomes are reported, with increased maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity [3]. Stillbirths and neonatal deaths are reported to be up to 50% higher for infants of adolescent mothers than for infants of women aged 20–29 years [1]. Babies born to adolescents are more likely to experience physical [4] and developmental issues [5] adding additional challenges. Immaturity of adolescents also places them at risk, socially and medically [6]. Much attention has been given to reducing adolescent pregnancy, but less focus on improving care and outcomes. We aim to develop a SSA-UK partnership to deliver a step change in care provided to adolescents by sharing expertise, accelerating research activity and translation, and providing a benchmark for high-quality healthcare in similar countries. Network activities will include learning and sharing events, workshops, community and stakeholder engagement, research priority setting and research protocol development. The proposed team will draw on research, midwifery, educational, social science, obstetrics, paediatrics and public health networks in the UK and SSA.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: SA-UK network for enhancing sign langauge interpreting in statutory health and social care.
descriptions: This proposed network is focussed on the estimated 400,000 Deaf users of South African Sign Language (SASL) who rely on interpreting services to access health and social work services.  Specifically, it focusses on the most serious circumstances when this might be required such at times of severe mental distress when the law permits assessment leading potentially to involuntary detention in psychiatric care or child protection investigations when parental rights are overtaken by the state and a child is removed. These high stakes situations are fundamentally dependent on effective communication yet effective support and guidance for health/social work professionals and SASL interpreters is not available.  The situation is highly complex given the vast language diversity of SA with most interpreters being multilinguals for whom neither the dominant spoken language nor the signed language are likely to be first languages. This project will map the field in real life, not theory.  It will bring together practitioners, Deaf people, interpreter trainers and academics to produce policy relevant evidence briefings and research papers that form the foundation for a later large-scale project as well as deliver immediate resources to enhance professional practice.  Through improving the working practices of practice professionals in the most seriously consequential interpreter mediated situations we are laying the foundations for improving practice across all healthcare access, reducing inequities of process and outcome for Deaf citizens and building the skills of the nascent SASL interpreting profession to the benefit of the quality of life all Deaf people in SA.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: South-East-North Network on Life Cycle Sustainability Assessment of Waste-to-Energy Technologies (SEN4WTE)
descriptions:
Brazil produces 80 million tonnes of solid waste annually and only 4% is reused or recycled. This creates a significant problem for the cities; however, it could be a good opportunity for Waste-to-Energy (WtE) technologies. Banana peels, for example, is a good feedstock for this thermochemical conversion due to the substantial volume of underutilized or improperly disposed agri-food residues. With more than 83 thousand tonnes of banana peels potentially generated every year, there is an opportunity to use this biomass through pyrolysis, a thermochemical process involves converting waste materials into valuable products and by-products. Extensive research is being conducted to understand the pyrolysis mechanisms for different types of waste and to enable their industrial-scale use. WtE technologies must prioritize achieving higher energy recovery efficiency, lower pollutant emissions, and positive impacts on societal well-being. However, there is a lack of comprehensive studies addressing the sustainability aspects of these technologies. Conducting socio-environmental assessments using a life cycle approach is essential to analyze the complete waste-to-energy value chain and provide comprehensive insights into the holistic sustainability aspects of these technologies.
This project aims to assess the socio-environmental aspects of an industrial-scale pyrolysis plant in Brazil through Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA). The waste used in this waste-to-energy system is banana peels. This project will contribute to disseminating the life cycle thinking, developing S-LCA, and adopting waste-to-energy technologies in Brazil. Furthermore, its outcomes can help inform public policies on renewable energy sources and promote a just energy transition.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: UK-Thai Health Alliance: Advancing Assistive and Rehabilitative Technology with Human-Centred Robotics and AI for Good Health and Well-being
descriptions:
Over 4 million people are experiencing physical disabilities in Thailand with the majority suffering from mobility impairments. The main causes are ageing-related muscle weakness, stroke, brain or spinal cord injuries due to road traffic accidents, and traumas from heavy manual work. Disability in Thailand leads to loss of work, poverty and living dependence. Medical treatments, rehabilitation facilities, and access to assistive devices are limited disproportionately in the rural and poorer communities where over 95% of disabled people in Thailand live. These combined factors result in unsustainable and unmet welfare and significantly reduced living quality of people with disabilities. 
This project will establish a new UK-Thai collaboration to generate innovative research ideas for advancing assistive and rehabilitative technology. Through networking events, meetings, visits, and workshops in both countries, we will foster knowledge exchange and skill transfer. We have brought together healthcare leaders with all necessary multidisciplinary expertise, including advanced soft robotics for comfortable medical devices (University of Bristol), artificial intelligence for intelligent human-centred control (Vidyasirimedhi Institute of Science and Technology), and specialists in physiotherapy and sports science for use-case analysis (Chulalongkorn University). This exciting collaboration will not only identify groundbreaking solutions to pressing healthcare challenges and stimulate technology advancement in Thailand, but it also lays the groundwork for a strong UK-Thai partnership to pursue larger collaborative research grants. Our ultimate goal is to translate our co-developed research ideas into innovative medical devices with high adaptability, technology acceptance, and trustworthiness, empowering individuals with efficient assistance and rehabilitation for improved health and well-being.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Bridging Global Nutrition Research: Advancing Approaches to Metabolic Health in Thailand-UK
descriptions:
Cardiometabolic diseases, such as heart disease, obesity, and diabetes are a growing global health concern. Nutritional manipulation, including dietary interventions like sugar and/or total carbohydrate restriction (e.g., ketogenic diets), and physical activity play a crucial role in managing and preventing these conditions. However, much of the research has been conducted in Western countries, with limited understanding of how these findings apply to populations in Southeast Asia, specifically Thailand.
This networking project is a first step towards addressing this gap by conducting region-specific studies on the effects of nutrient composition in Thai populations. The project is a collaboration between researchers at Chulabhorn Royal Academy in Thailand and the University of Bath, UK, leveraging UK expertise to develop high-quality human nutrition research in Thailand. Through bi-lateral visits and workshops, we plan to transfer expertise on conducting replicate crossover randomized controlled trials to generate data that can inform public health guidelines tailored to Thai communities. The lead applicant will conduct a pilot study aligned with UK co-applicants, generating data which would allow us to apply for larger funding providing much-needed data on how individuals from diverse backgrounds respond to dietary interventions, helping to create more inclusive health recommendations. The potential impact is significant, as this research will improve public health outcomes in Thailand and contribute to global efforts to develop culturally sensitive nutrition guidelines.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: INDIGO: International Network Development in Indonesia for GOnorrhoea surveillance
descriptions:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) is a major cause of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and a contributor to HIV transmission. Ng has developed significant resistance to antibiotics, making it harder to treat. To combat this, advanced methods like whole genome sequencing (WGS) are essential, as WGS provides valuable insights into how the bacteria spread, evolve and develop resistance. However, most WGS studies have been conducted in wealthy countries with little to no data from low-and-middle-income countries including Indonesia where gonorrhoea cases are rising. 
This project aims to build a network of Ng research and surveillance capacity in Indonesia. Through a combination of symposia, networking activities and training workshops, we will build the capacity in Indonesia for studying Ng ranging from sample collection techniques, to improving laboratory expertise to developing WGS capabilities. In the long-term, this will help identify resistance patterns and potential vaccine candidates while also boosting the country's ability to monitor and respond to infections. The project will gather clinicians, public health officials and researchers located in Central and Western Java, over time expanding across Indonesia. It will support global efforts to track and manage gonorrhoea which is a significant cause of health issues including infertility and chronic pain in women. The development of the INDIGO consortium will contribute to the World Health Organisation's Ng surveillance program and will forge a pathway in making Ng WGS studies accessible in Indonesia.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Establishing an international consortium to developing interventions, initially for parents of children with suicidality and/or self-harm in low-middl
descriptions:
This project focuses on helping parents support children and young people (CYP) who self-harm or experience suicidal thoughts. We focus on Brazil, Rwanda, and Malaysia, where this problem is increasing, but resources are limited. Most research and interventions so far have taken place in high-income, “Western” countries, leaving a gap in knowledge about how best to help families in low-income settings, which we seek to address. 
Our overall objective is to develop interventions for these parents, simultaneously across the three settings, based on a shared blue-print, with locally relevant variations. This exciting approach will allow efficient shared learning. The network activities develop the methodological and foundational work. 
We will bring together experts and stakeholders in each setting to understand locally experienced needs, existing resources, ideas for intervention, and barriers to intervention implementation, informed by interviews with key-informant health-care professionals and establishment of Parent and Young Person Advisory Groups. Supported by our ongoing literature review, an international meeting will include skill-sharing between and building, and development of the blue-print, and a research plan to develop and evaluate interventions from that blue-print, but tailored to local settings. 
Our proposed work is unique in focus on parents and methodology of shared learning during intervention development across settings. The skills building and stakeholder connections will lay foundations for work on other mental health challenges. Whilst we focus on issues around self-harm and suicidality, our approach and learning can be generalised to other areas of young people’s mental health.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Indonesia-UK healthy pregnancy journey (IUPJ) network
descriptions: The ‘Indonesia-UK healthy pregnancy journey (IUPJ) network' aims to bring together midwifery and psychology practitioners and researchers in the two countries to better understand how to support a mentally and physically healthy pregnancy. Having a mentally and physically healthy pregnancy creates a healthy family and has potential impact for the wider society. However, not all women have a healthy pregnancy, something the applicants think is unfair. The applicants hope the network will work with everyone involved in pregnancy such as midwives and doctors as well as pregnant women and their families to reduce these inequalities. All of these important people will be involved in all the work. The applicants have experience of working with researchers from the other country so understand the important role of psychology and midwifery in a healthy pregnancy journey and want to further develop this collaboration. Increasing understanding about what makes a healthy pregnancy will help to improve care for women and the working environment for professionals.
