process, and in the long run increase the number of women in the
e-mobility entrepreneurship value chain, impacting the individual, societal
and economic wellbeing."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: StrokeDT: Early Intervention for Minor Stroke Patients in Vietnam and Indonesia using Digital Twinning
descriptions:
"Vietnam and Indonesia face a pressing healthcare challenge of increasing
burden of stroke, exacerbated by delayed hospitalisation for minor stroke
patients, often due to mild initial symptoms. This research proposal seeks
to harness cutting-edge digital twin (DT) technology with integrated
machine learning models to enable real-time monitoring, prediction of
subsequent major strokes and swift intervention for patients upon hospital
admission. The project aims to develop, rigorously test, and validate this
innovative approach at the Bach Mai Stroke Centre in Hanoi and other
major hospitals in Vietnam and Indonesia.
Our interdisciplinary team, spanning the UK, Vietnam and Indonesia,
comprises experts from diverse fields, such as engineers, clinicians,
physicians, and researchers. The leading UK partner, the London Digital
Twin Research Centre at Middlesex University, brings extensive
experience in DT development, previously applied across various domains,
to advance stroke care and prediction. Collaborating closely clinicians
affiliated with multiple stroke centres and hospitals in Vietnam and
Indonesia is key for data collection and modelling. Additionally,
contributions from experienced stroke and neuroscience researchers at
University of Oxford (UK), Vietnam National University (VNU) and
Universitas Gadjah Mada (Indonesia), enhance the project with the
cross-country expertise in stroke detection and interventions.
Collectively, we integrate cutting-edge DT with frontline clinical experience,
promising a ground-breaking approach to stroke detection. To foster
international collaboration and knowledge sharing, the team will organise
workshops and lectures, and seek collaboration with the local Ministry of
Health to integrate research outcomes into policy and decision-making. The
project technical and clinical outcomes offer scalable models that can be
applied to stroke centres worldwide, potentially revolutionising stroke care
on a global scale." The expected outcomes directly contribute to the improvement of health and well-being within DAC-listed countries. Through enhanced stroke care, early intervention, and advanced research, we anticipate a substantial reduction in stroke-related mortality/disabilities, fostering healthier and more prosperous societies. This project holds the potential for collaboration with world-leading research centres. In essence, it not only aligns with ODA funding requirements but also underlines a concerted effort to create a lasting positive impact.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Eco-Creative Pedagogies: Training the Next Generation of Teachers on Green Skills and Resilience
descriptions: This project seeks to address the theme of planetary resilience by fostering a collaborative network among schools, teachers, eco-artists, environmental activists, and think-tanks, as well as non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in both the UK and Turkey. Our goal is to bring these diverse stakeholders together to facilitate mutual learning and the exchange of effective practices, with a particular emphasis on enhancing green skills in educational settings through innovative, eco-creative approaches. This initiative is designed to elevate ecological consciousness and integrate sustainable practices into educational curricula, drawing upon the ERG’s foundational work in ecological education and its established networks, including the Teachers’ network and UK team’s research on decolonial and eco-creative pedagogies in teaching climate change in UK schools.  By creating synergies between these existing groups, we aim to co-develop a comprehensive teacher training programme. This programme will empower teachers with the necessary skills and methodologies to teach environmental awareness innovatively and creatively. Our approach addresses the critical need for culturally responsive educational frameworks and alternative, eco-artistic pedagogical strategies to equip learners with the knowledge, skills, and values necessary to act as stewards of the environment and inspire a sense of responsibility to contribute to a resilient planet.  The project is structured in two phases: the first involves knowledge exchange, synergy creation, and collaborative learning among participants. The second phase focuses on the development and implementation of teacher training programmes, which aim to teach, integrate, and promote green skills within Turkish schools, culminating in the creation of a co-designed comic book for children to build up resilience capacity and response to climate crisis. This training will be disseminated through a robust network, including networks and grassroots teacher groups such as the Teachers’ Network, which has  over 10,000 teacher members in Turkey. It will be supported by continuous professional development (CPD) resources and offered in both in-person and online formats to ensure wide accessibility.  In the long term, the project aims to train next-generation of teachers on climate crisis and strengthen and build their resilience to cope with the climate crisis, fostering ongoing dialogue and collaboration between UK and Turkey to integrate critical environmental competencies broadly into civil society, thereby contributing to the resilience of our planet.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Rainfall frequency models for critical infrastructure design in a changing environment
descriptions:
"The project is a new collaboration between UK and Turkey partners, aimed
at strengthening the evidence-base for frequency analysis of extreme
rainfall under climate change and thus supporting the resilience of critical
infrastructure (e.g. flood defences and energy installations) in both
countries. Frequency analysis of extreme rainfall events relies on
Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves which are underpinned by
statistical extreme value models. IDF curves have traditionally been
developed assuming a stationarity climate; an assumption which is no
longer realistic due to climate change. Hence, there is a need for
development of new and non-stationary IDF curve models to support
mitigation and adaptation to future extreme events. In this project, we will
develop a new class of non-stationary IDF curve models where model
parameters are informed by physical covariates linked to large-scale
atmospheric processes obtained from global and regional climate models.
The research is building on existing datasets and recent scientific
developments and innovations into non-stationary models undertaken by
each group. Successful outcome of the project will enable end-users
(engineers and hydrologists) to predict the likely change in magnitude and
frequency of extreme events under climate change. The results will be
disseminated through guidance documents for operational engineers as
well as scientific publications."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Enhancing Post-Earthquake Communication Resilience The Integration of UAVs, LoRa Technology, and GDPR-Compliant Systems
descriptions:
"Introducing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in disaster response and recovery operations has transformed how we handle post-disaster scenarios, particularly if the traditional communication infrastructures are damaged or destroyed. UAVs are flexible, mobile, and can be rapidly deployed, making them essential for establishing communication networks in disaster areas. This research aims to combine the benefits of UAVs with LoRa technology, known for its long-range and low-power capabilities, and ensure data protection as required by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The goal is to create a resilient and secure mobile network specifically designed for use after earthquakes.

The motivation behind this research is the urgent need to establish reliable and dynamic communication channels during disaster recovery efforts. Effective communication can significantly reduce the overall impact of catastrophic events by enabling timely coordination among rescue teams, efficient allocation of resources, and quick dissemination of crucial information.

Post-disaster environments are challenging due to constantly changing conditions and limited resources. To tackle these challenges, we will employ strategies to extend the network’s lifespan, maintain service quality, and ensure compliance with GDPR security protocols. A central part of this research is developing a practical prototype to test our solutions in real-world scenarios. This prototype will allow comprehensive testing and evaluation of our communication methods, providing valuable insights into their performance and effectiveness in disaster recovery operations. We will use a combination of theoretical modelling, simulation, and practical experimentation to achieve our goals.
Our research methods include several innovative strategies. First, we will use network situational awareness to implement load balancing and UAV trajectory-based forwarding protocols. These protocols aim to optimise data routing, ensuring efficient resource use and enhancing overall network performance. Second, we will investigate self-organising UAV swarm mechanisms using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques. These mechanisms will enable UAVs to dynamically adjust their positions and coverage areas, ensuring optimal network coverage and connectivity. Additionally, we will explore edge computing techniques for decentralised data processing. We can reduce latency and improve data handling and analysis efficiency by processing data at the network’s edge, closer to the data sources. This approach is crucial in disaster scenarios where timely decision-making is essential.

Equipping UAVs with cellular, LoRa, satellite communications, and GDPR-compliant systems significantly enhances disaster response. This robust, secure network facilitates faster recovery, better resource management, and improved rescue team coordination, ultimately mitigating disaster impacts and accelerating community recovery.

In summary, this research aims to advance disaster recovery communication networks by integrating UAV technology with LoRa, edge computing, AI, and GDPR-compliant security protocols. The development and testing of these innovative communication methods aim to provide a reliable and resilient solution for post-disaster scenarios. The broader impact includes enhanced disaster response, improved recovery times, and better resource management, contributing to societal and economic resilience in the face of natural disasters. This project will significantly impact various stakeholders by improving disaster preparedness and response capabilities, including individuals, organisations, and nations."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Evidence based support for improving the sustainability of native poultry in Indonesia
descriptions:
"Chickens are the most numerous food animals in the world. The importance of the chicken as a food animal continues to grow based on its comparatively low cost, high growth efficiency, and health and environmental benefits over red meat. Chickens are also a crucial source of income for smallholders in developing nations, providing farmers (often women) with financial autonomy and security. In Indonesia, indigenous chickens make up the vast majority of smallholding chicken flocks, with regional preferences for different local breeds. However, there is still much to be learned about these indigenous breeds.
Through a collaboration between the University of Oxford (UK) and Universitas Sebelas Maret (Indonesia), we seek to thoroughly investigate Indonesian native chickens, both from a phenotypic (physical characteristics) and a genotypic (genetics) perspective. Sampling chickens from diverse locations across Indonesian islands and sequencing their genomes, we will assess the ‘genetic health’ of different indigenous breeds, or the degree to which each breed is affected by inbreeding. Since different breeds are prized for their distinct physical characteristics, we will study the genetic basis of these traits. Understanding the genetic composition of Indonesian chickens provides the foundations on which chicken breeds can be improved for enhanced productivity for eggs or meat through targeted breeding programmes. The Indonesian scientists in this proposal are already deeply embedded within local communities and within both provincial and national government, so have the means to effect real change. Improvements made to the productivity of these chicken breeds will have direct and meaningful impacts on the smallholders themselves, as well as the provincial economy and the wider poultry industry across Indonesia. Identifying breeds with poor genetic health will also help to define conservation priorities within Indonesia, generating momentum to protect genetically vulnerable breeds with significant local value.
Since infectious diseases can cause severe losses to poultry farmers, we will also screen chickens for a highly virulent tumour-causing virus – Marek’s Disease Virus (MDV). MDV disproportionately affects the poorest poultry producers since they are unable to purchase the protective vaccine or afford to purchase commercial birds with intrinsic MDV resistance. While it is known that MDV circulates in Indonesia, the extent to which virulent strains cause significant losses is unclear. We will roll out a programme of MDV screening, identifying populations and regions which are affected by MDV. Through whole-genome sequencing of the virus, we will be able to detect the presence of virulent MDV strains in Indonesia. We will also begin to understand how the virus is evolving in the country by identifying locations in the MDV genome which are changing rapidly under positive selection. This work will benefit smallholders by identifying MDV threats in their local area, by providing education about disease control measures, and by identifying chicken breeds which are naturally more resistant to infection. Using this knowledge, farmers will be able to make informed decisions about how best to manage their chickens to optimise the productivity, health and welfare of their flocks."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Integrating Polarized Light in AI-driven Biophotonics: Enhancing Health Applications (iPOL-Bio)
descriptions:
"With the current amount of limited resources, the present health-care
system could only meet 30% to 40% of the demand for cancer services in
Vietnam. The iPOL-Bio initiative, spearheaded by Aston University in
collaboration with a Vietnamese International University - Vietnam National
University (VNU-HCM), aims to significantly ease the healthcare and
patient burden in Vietnam, in line with the country's sustainable healthcare
objectives. This project introduces the iPOL-Bio system, integrating
polarized light and AI in biophotonics for non-invasive, immediate cancer
detection and categorization. It echoes Vietnam's healthcare innovation
ambitions, elevating the country in the global fight against cancer through
advanced technology. Additionally, Aston's involvement will extend to
enhancing Vietnam's cancer diagnosis and treatment capabilities, aiming to
lessen the financial impact on patients and their families, thus improving
their life quality and affirming Vietnam's status in healthcare innovation.
This initiative is expected to draw more international collaborations and
investments."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: C-Bio-Living Lab: Circular Solutions for Food, Energy and Water Nexus in Jordan
descriptions: Food-waste management and nutrient losses, rising energy costs and water scarcity are challenges for agri-food resilience across Jordan. Building on the previous RAEng Frontiers-funded Green Nexus pilot that has already integrated anaerobic digestion (AD) and hydroponics at the Royal Scientific Society (RSS) with University of Sheffield (UoS) expertise, we propose a Circular Bio-Hydroponics Living Lab (C-Bio-Lab) to demonstrate, validate and mainstream closed-loop food–energy–nutrient systems in Jordan. We address the thematic priority area of Resilient Planet while nurturing  the cross-cutting theme of Tomorrow’s Talent. The project will be interdisciplinary, combining expertise from plants science, environmental biotechnology, process modelling and food security.  The project will (i) upgrade and expand the existing pilot into a showcase facility hosted by the “Jordan Valley Development and Reconstruction Cooperative Society” NGO in the Jordan Valley and co-developed with local biogas and hydroponics SMEs. It will incorporate vermifiltration of digestate, biogas use as a green energy source for different domestic purposes, and modular “organic” hydroponic units; (ii) run controlled experiments at RSS and UoS on crop selection and nutrient balancing to optimise yield and food safety; (iii) co-create an open “design toolkit” linking biogas potential, nutrient flows, energy balances, enabling planners and SMEs to test “what-if” deployment scenarios, informed by pilot data and best-practice literature on digestate-based hydroponics; and (iv) deliver gender-balanced stakeholder workshops in Jordan, Sheffield and online to refine business models, policy pathways and skills needs, foregrounding early-career researchers and circular-economy SMEs from both countries. Expected outputs include: 1) a fully-instrumented living lab open to new graduates (plant scientists, engineers, microbiologists), farmers, women-led cooperatives and start-ups for hands-on training in Jordan - on the topic of: anaerobic digestion, hydroponics, bioresources management, business development; 2) design & operation guidelines that correlates the food waste inputs with a well-characterized digestate outputs,agronomic recommendations and cost-revenue blueprints 3) an open-access design support toolkit 4) a co-authored journal paper and one policy brief 5) a cohort of early-career researchers and practitioners mentored through the project, directly addressing the call’s Tomorrow’s Talent cross-cutting theme.  Workshops and knowledge-sharing events will be held in Jordan and the UK to ensure the involvement of women, youth, farmers, agricultural engineers, start-ups, and early-career researchers. These events will focus on developing business models for the food waste digestate as a free resource, utilization of natural fertilizers and green energy sources, identifying policy needs, and building the skills required to scale up circular solutions in agriculture. Overall, the project will de-risk adoption of circular bio-hydroponics, create new green-skills jobs, and lay the groundwork for an enduring RSS–UoS hub capable of attracting further bilateral investment. By transforming unavoidable food waste into renewable energy, climate-smart fertiliser and high-value produce, C-Bio-Lab will advance SDGs 2, 5, 7 and 11, and contribute to Jordan’s National Green Growth Plan.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: UK-Jordan Centre for AI-Driven Early Warning System for Climate-Resilient Agriculture
descriptions: Jordan faces critical challenges in agriculture due to climate change, water scarcity, and land degradation. To address these issues, this UK–Jordan collaborative research initiative proposes the development and piloting of an AI-powered Early Warning System (EWS) for climate-resilient agriculture. The system will integrate satellite remote sensing data, ground-based IoT sensors, and advanced machine learning algorithms to monitor and predict crop stress, drought risk, and soil moisture variability. The overarching goal is to empower farmers, policymakers, and water managers with real-time, predictive insights that support adaptive decision-making, optimise water use, reduce crop losses, and enhance resilience to climate extremes. However, Jordan suffers from a chronic lack of technological capacity, facilities, infrastructure, and systems necessary to manage and adopt Artificial Intelligence solutions within its agricultural sector. There is an urgent need to build capacity for implementing smart early warning systems and to support the development of new models of global climate resilience. With the growing influence of AI and Machine learning on the use and development of smart agricultural systems, scientists and agricultural professionals must develop greater awareness, critical skills, and access to digital and AI technology and methods to protect food security and environmental sustainability. To this end, Jordan's AI and machine learning protocols for its vast agricultural sites are in urgent need of sustainable research and technological know-how to support local professionals in scientific innovation and the digital transformation of its hundreds of agricultural sites across the country. This includes connecting its current Agricultural sites to a unified warning system across Jordan, utilising machine learning and AI-enabled applications, as well as remote sensing technologies for monitoring and predictive analysis. The proposed project will establish an international Centre of Excellence in AI and early warning technologies, building capacity in technology acquisition, cloud-based processing, and remote sensing applications that support the systematic recording, monitoring, and AI-enabled recognition of Agricultural sites in Jordan. The Centre builds on Professors Selim and Shantawi's award-winning conceptual framework for AI technology, activating the potential of AI and machine learning for climate resilience and sustainable development in Jordan. The Centre is a natural development of sustainable and long-term research partnerships between research institutions and stakeholders in Jordan and the UK. The Centre will be run collaboratively by the University of Leeds and Al-Balqa Applied University to build capacity in equipment, software, digital systems, knowledge exchange and training programmes.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Empower Women Entrepreneurs in Türkiye Post-2023 Earthquake Through Digital Capacity Building and Adopting Digital Solutions to Support Business Growt
descriptions: The world is facing a myriad of crises, including natural disasters, outbreaks of contagious diseases, and the increasing impacts of climate change, which disproportionately affect communities. On 6 February 2023, a series of earthquakes centred in Kahramanmaraş, in South Türkiye, affecting 11 provinces. Hatay has been the most affected province with 48,422 businesses being destroyed. Among those severely impacted were Women Entrepreneurs (WE), running Micro, Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (MSMEs). Based on UN Women report (2023), following the earthquake in Türkiye, 88% of women entrepreneurs including refugees had their business operations affected, while 50% who took a break stated that they could not resume production and/or services post-earthquake. Furthermore, the key supports for their success has been identified as promotion and market support, as well as management and counselling support.   The ‘ELEVATE’ Project aims to develop, implement and evaluate, a digital capacity-building toolkit to empower women-led MSMEs in Hatay, post2023 earthquake, supporting sustainable business growth and economic recovery in disaster-affected regions. Assisting women entrepreneurs in building digital capacity, deploying marketing-related business solutions, and enhancing their sustainable competitive advantage and business survival.   The core methodology employed for ELEVATE is Open Innovation and Design principles1) Discover 2) Define 3) Develop and 4) Deliver. Through consistent consultation and co-creation wit WE via six work packages, ELEVATE will conduct a digital literacy gap analysis, develop strategies and resources to address these gaps, implement the solutions and monitor their impact on the WE businesses. WE of MSMEs will be further supported and monitored to evaluate the impacts as they could be role models for the others. In doing so, a Community of Practice (CoPs) called “ELEVATE-CoPs” will be formed. This CoPs will initially be in Hatay and then expanded to other parts of  severely affected by the earthquake, such as Kahramanmaraş and Gaziantep as short to medium term impact. This will create regional and national level CoPs.  ELEVATE is led by the University of Wolverhampton (UoW) and its Centre for International Development and Training (CIDT) with its 50-year track record in capacity strengthening across 120 countries. Türkiye’s lead partner is Cappadocia University (KUN).   ELEVATE’ is supported by 4 associated partners which will support the delivery and long-term impacts of the project.   1) Tech West Midlands (TechWM), UK 2) Mustafa Kemal University (HMKU), Türkiye 3) CARE International (CI), Türkiye 4)  Women Entrepreneurs Production and Management Cooperative (Antiokhia), Türkiye.   The project team consists of experienced researchers, whose work has influenced economic development in more than 30 countries, as well as Early Career Researchers (ECRs).   The impact of ELEVATE extends beyond academic research, benefiting various stakeholders including WE, the local community, and policymakers. The project along with support to WE also contribute to broader goals of economic growth and social innovation, creating a more inclusive and resilient business ecosystem focused on effective marketing strategies, innovative business models for sustainability and knowledge leadership for optimisation in services. This rebuilding will contribute to Türkiye ’s post-earthquake economic recovery, growth, promoting gender equality in entrepreneurship, fostering a more inclusive business environment.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Sharing Best Practice for Neurodivergent Students and Staff in Higher Education - Development of international knowledge base and inclusive strategies
descriptions:
"With only 40% of Indonesia's labour are skilled workers and ~1.85million
college/university graduates, Indonesia aspires to revolutionising higher
educations (HE) in order to meet the 113million skilled professional's target
by 2030. One of the Indonesia's Ministry of Education and Culture (MoEC)
strategies is to embrace neurodiversity (ND). From 2,316 HE institutions
(391 universities) across Indonesia; only ~2% offers limited and
'nonspecific to ND' disability support [MoEC, 2022].
The transition to HE is a pivotal time for neurodivergent students, many of
whom have developed sophisticated coping strategies since childhood that
masked their conditions and eluded diagnosis. These strategies can
crumble due to increased independence and exposure to HE
fields/environment; deriving the needs of cultural shifts, interventions, and
transformations from traditional (didactic) ways of teaching and learnings,
assessment and feedback. British Psychological Society reveals 1-in-7 UK
HE students are neurodivergent with increasing cases upon entering HE;
whilst only 15% neurodivergent workforces are accounted for (Wise
Campaign, 2023). Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), among many UK
universities, have established disability (including ND) supports for students
and staff.
ARU and Sampoerna University will embark in this knowledge exchange
project aiming at mainstreaming and capacity building in
neurodiverse-inclusive education (NIE) in HE. Leveraging interdisciplinary
research in social science, pedagogy for ND and engineering education,
we will develop a Knowledge Base consisting of methodologies to
recognise ND, best practices derived from national and international
policies, and strategies for tailoring curriculum/syllabus for NIE. By utilizing
regional research networks and partners in HE, we envisage forming an
International Research and Networking in Neurodiverse-Inclusive
Education (IRNNIE) Group to furthering and sustaining the research and
impacts to society."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of precision medicine-based antihypertensive therapy for controlling cardiovascular disease risks in rural populations in Indonesia
descriptions:
"Stroke and heart attack are major health problems in Indonesia. High blood
pressure (hypertension) is one major risk factor for stroke and heart attack.
Our study showed that more than half of the people age >40 years old in
the rural areas of Malang District, Indonesia, have high blood pressure, but
surprisingly, a significant proportion of them did not respond well to
antihypertensive medications. We hypothesised that the response to
antihypertensive drugs is associated with genetic variations, and if we can
establish a method to rapidly detect such variations, then we can determine
the best type of medication that can be given to people with hypertension.
In this study, we will determine genetic variations that are associated with
the response to antihypertensive drugs in the rural population of Malang
District, Indonesia. We will then develop a simple method for the detection
of such genetic variations that can be applied in areas with limited
laboratory facilities. We will also conduct workshops and training for
healthcare workers in the Malang area to inform and train them on the use
of molecular diagnostic tools to improve the effectiveness of drugs and
medications and to diagnose other common diseases.
This approach, which is called personalised medicine, can help improve the
effectiveness of therapy and reduce the unnecessary healthcare budget
due to ineffective treatment. Overall, our project will be beneficial in
improving health and increasing quality of life, as well as reducing
unnecessary medications."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Improving the competitiveness of low impact tilapia production in Thailand
descriptions:
"Tilapia is one the most consumed and affordable aquatic foods in Thailand.
Government support and a vibrant private sector have driven growth over
the last forty years since the emergence of improved strains, formulated
feed and improved management. Production systems range from intensive
cage-based systems to semi-intensive pond-based polycultures, delivering
aquatic products at higher and lower ends of price respectively. There is
also an emerging opportunity to expand into brackish water ponds, vacated
by the shrimp industry. Thailand's innovation in the tilapia sector has led to
it becoming a centre for training, knowledge and hardware for countries
initiating their own tilapia sectors, elsewhere in the Global South.
The Thai sector now appears to have plateaued in production due to
competition from higher trophic species (e.g. Asian Sea bass) and imported
fish (e.g. farmed salmon) and remains uncompetitive in export markets.
Innovation is urgently required, as recognised by the Tilapia Association of
Thailand, a local organisation led by major hatcheries of high quality
juveniles. They have all invested in selective breeding programmes but
comparable performance in different grow-out systems and in terms of
sustainability metrics remains unknown. Such information if co-created in a
pre-competitive approach would add value to the sector supporting
strategic investment and capacity for making and validating green claims
required to promote the fish locally and in export markets.
This proposal aims to partner with a Thai University (KMUTT) with a
credible record in sustainability assessments, to support innovation in the
Thai tilapia sector by defining a baseline of environmental impact across
production systems. The project will co-develop business and investment
strategies for boosting local consumption and strategic exports that will
support the development of Thailand as a tilapia innovation hub with an
expected multiplier impact throughout the Global South."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Building Capacity in Molecular Diagnostics and Developing a Personalised Health Message to Mitigate the Burden of Gestational Urinary Tract Infection
descriptions:
"We have a record of partnership work through our initial collaborative project with funding from the Global Challenges Research Fund (GCRF) and conducted during the COVID-19 social distancing public health measures, which explored the risk factors associated with susceptibility and severity of a common pregnancy infection, urinary Tract Infection (UTI) among pregnant women in Kisumu. In the project, we observed a higher rate of multi-drug resistance associated with UTI. UTI is a major contributory factor to maternal infection in pregnant women in Kisumu. A higher rate of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) in maternal infections further compromised the antibiotic treatment of maternal and neonatal infections in this community. Our findings lead to the conclusion that the importance of effective identification, awareness and management of UTI will reduce the burden of AMR and the associated maternal and newborn deaths in this region.

The ISPF further strengthens the established partnership between the UK and Kenya. The ISPF funding will be utilised to build the capacity of effective diagnostic methods, create a personalised health message on a common pregnancy infection, and raise awareness and management of this common infection. Traditional UTI diagnostic methods in this region often miss early signs of infection, leading to serious health risks for mothers and babies. Using advanced molecular techniques like quantitative PCR (qPCR) and next-generation sequencing (NGS), the project will train a researcher from MU and a medical laboratory technologist from the Ministry of Health to accurately identify UTI-causing bacteria. The training will enhance diagnostic capabilities in Kisumu County, ensuring quicker targeted treatment and reducing complications such as preterm birth and maternal infections.

The proposed project will also develop culturally sensitive self-care advice on managing UTIs based on the previously gathered information on the population characteristics of pregnant women. This tailored health message will educate pregnant women about UTI symptoms, risks, and the importance of timely medical care. Furthermore, we will assess the efficacy of the developed health message through a county hospital audit by analysing pre and post-intervention antibiotic prescription data (post-project). By promoting responsible antibiotic use, the initiative aims to combat AMR, a global health threat exacerbated by the overuse of antibiotics.

Potential impact beyond academia
The ISPF collaboration’s impact will be felt directly by individuals through improved health outcomes and better access to accurate diagnoses. Healthcare providers such as the Ministry of Health in Kisumu County and the MU will benefit from enhanced diagnostic capabilities, potentially reducing costs associated with prolonged treatments and hospital stays. At a national level, the project aligns with WHO’s global health priorities to improve maternal health and combat AMR.

The research’s broader significance lies in its potential to serve as a model for similar regions in Kenya and other sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries, demonstrating how advanced diagnostics and targeted education can transform healthcare outcomes in resource-limited settings. By empowering local healthcare professionals and educating communities, the project contributes to sustainable health practices and economic stability, ultimately benefiting society by improving maternal and child health."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Strengthening Cyber Resilience and Navigational Safety in Turkish Straits: Development and Testing of Prevention Strategies in Simulated Environments
descriptions:
"In digital transformation era, the importance of cybersecurity has
significantly increased. As mentioned in DNV's (Det Norske Veritas) report,
76% of industry experts predict that cyber-attacks would likely result in the
closure of strategic waterways. Therefore, maritime organisations must
adapt strategically to evolving digital threats. Hazardous cargoes such as
crude oil, liquefied gas, ammonia, chemical products, and radioactive
materials are transported by numerous vessels crossing the Turkish Straits,
which include the Istanbul Strait in the north, the Sea of Marmara, and the
Çanakkale Strait in the south.
The introduction of autonomous vessels and the transition to alternative
fuels for decarbonisation are expected to increase the risks linked with
navigating the Turkish Straits, the only maritime route connecting the Black
Sea states. Therefore Istanbul and the Turkish Straits region, home to
more than 20 million people, including the many historical structures along
the shoreline, are at a higher risk of maritime accidents caused by cyber
threats. Hackers can take control of the ship's integrated bridge system and
operate it. Thus, cyberattacks can interrupt navigation, cause physical
damage, and harm ship operators, the economy, and the environment.
This project proposes using AI-based risk modelling to investigate and
model the potential outcomes of maritime cyber-attack risks in the Turkish
Straits. It emphasises the importance of human-machine interface (HMI)
within a simulation environment to avert catastrophic incidents. Partnering
with Istanbul Technical University (ITU) in this new collaboration, we aim to
identify and evaluate cyber threats targeting maritime vessels in the Turkish
Straits, assessing the vulnerability of critical systems to cyber attacks. This
novel method combines human involvement with resilience strategies to
overcome the lack of cyber risk studies in vital waterways and provides a
substantial contribution to the field."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: The Interplay Between Genetic Perturbations and Tissue Microenvironment in Chronic Liver Diseases and Liver Cancer
descriptions: Liver cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is the malignant transformation of hepatocytes and accounts for around 80% of total liver cancer cases. The current management options for HCC include receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitors with limited options of immunotherapies compared to other tumour types. Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is an emerging cause of non-viral HCC. Changes in DNA sequence (mutations) can lead to the activation of certain genes (oncogenes) or lessening the protective impact of others (tumour suppressor genes) and are key drivers of HCC development and progression. P53 is a tumour-suppressor gene that senses and regulates DNA damage response, cellular metabolism, and cell cycle. Point mutation(s) within the P53 DNA sequence shifts the cell’s behaviour towards malignancy and tumour P53 or TP53 is prevalent in HCC as in other cancers, often with poor patient outcome. To date, no data is available regarding the link between genetic determinants and/or rare variants and the development of MAFLD and liver cancer in the Egyptian population, most probably because of the lack of systematic storage and processing of human samples in the Egyptian hospitals. Limited research resources and funding opportunities are major obstacles for young Egyptian basic science researchers, especially in underserved areas where limited training options affect vulnerable groups. Through building a consortium that involves the University of Birmingham, UK and Faculties of Pharmacy and Medicine at Minia University and Deraya University, Egypt, this project builds on the previous two Newton-funded projects to improve basic and clinical research capabilities in Upper Egypt, introduce a new registry and biorepository for the most demanding liver diseases in Egypt, and pave the way for international collaboration in the health sector to achieve personalised medicine in chronic liver diseases and liver cancer. The project will also deepen the existing basic science knowledge about the key metabolic and immune modulators of liver tissue/tumour tissue microenvironment. This will highlight novel therapeutic targets that fit with the new era of ”personalised medicine” in patients with chronic liver diseases and liver cancer. Most importantly, this project will build stronger relations between the Egyptian and UK institutions to achieve the SDGs concerned with healthy people, quality education, innovation and industry, and partnership for goals.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: PASIG Healthcare: Pharmaceutical Pollution Assessment to foster Systems Innovation and Governance in Healthcare
descriptions:
"Healthcare remains inaccessible to many socio-economically deprived
Filipinos, resulting in high levels of self-medication including inappropriate
use of antimicrobials, which can drive antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a
threat to health and productivity. The nascent Universal Healthcare Act of
the Philippine government will widen access to diagnosis, may increase
appropriate prescription, and may decrease inappropriate use of
antimicrobials. Net consequences for pharmaceutical pollution and AMR
risk are therefore unpredictable and baseline data lacking. Current
behaviors and attitudes, which may be gender specific, towards disease
management and (antimicrobial) pharmaceutical use and disposal in the
Philippines are also largely unknown, hindering evidence-based policy
development.
Our proposal aims to investigate the complex social and behavioral factors
that contribute to antimicrobials pollution along Pasig River in Metro Manila
and co-design local systems-based solutions that will help mitigate this
health and environmental issue. Using a transdisciplinary approach, we
will: 1) conduct stakeholder mapping with social and behavioral key
informant interviews on antimicrobial use and disposal; 2) conduct the
first-ever targeted monitoring campaign to identify hotspots of antimicrobial
pollution and AMR-related risks; and 3) conduct scenario-planning with key
stakeholders to co-design an innovation roadmap for health and social
wellbeing, a sustainable pharmaceutical industry, increased productivity,
and strengthening of the blue economy through rehabilitated ecosystems.
With commitment from the Philippine and UK governments to the COP28
Health Declaration, and UK support to the full-scale implementation of the
Philippine's Universal Healthcare Act, this project envisages to support the
Philippines towards its transition to a sustainable, resilient, and universal
healthcare system."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: "Resilient & Green Healthcare in Egypt: Development of AI aided Optimal Electrothermal Energy Management Strategy design software for Healthcare facil
descriptions:
Amidst the global green transition movement towards utilising environmentally friendly technology and facilities, Egypt is also committed to advancing green energy technologies and facilities. This aligns with Egypt's 2030 vision to deliver an eco-friendly healthcare system nationwide. This project aims to develop green healthcare facilities by reducing thermal and electrical loads to decrease energy consumption, generating in-house
green energy by PV systems installation, and integrating battery energy storage to support the critical loads in hospitals during scheduled and
unscheduled blackouts. These objectives are achievable individually using software like Ansys, PVSyst & Homer, but that endeavour requires the involvement of multiple software and engineers to work collaboratively to come up with a unified solution. This project aims to remove this barrier by developing a unified software solution in Matlab, streaming the process into a single phase and focused on healthcare facilities.
The developed software package will design strategies to reduce thermal and electrical loads depending on building criteria. Secondly, it will optimise PV system and battery storage requirements considering the dynamic load and blackout profiles, and thermal load variations over the healthcare facility's lifespan. Machine Learning (ML) models will forecast solar energy, load and blackout profiles to optimise the solution. This software will also predict battery life degradation, replacement schedule, and provide levelized energy cost for long operation periods. This information will aid engineers to deploy efficient designs and strategies for a greener facility. Besides, it will assist the business team in making the sustainable decisions for economic facility operation." Our project aligns with the Egypt's government's vision 2030 and goal of ensuring citizen welfare and fostering sustainable green healthcare services. We aim to achieve this by implementing various project activities, developing strategies to reduce the thermal load, optimal sizing of PV and backup energy systems in healthcare facilities. Through the creation of the software, we will provide an optimal solution tailored to the specific needs of the healthcare sector in Egypt. Additionally, the developed software could be adapted in other sectors in Egypt to determine the appropriate pathways in achieving green facilities. Such achievement will reduce Egypt's dependency on conventional fossil fuels and their carbon footprint. Besides, this project will help the healthcare sector to be resilient to face the prospective energy shortage and blackouts, particularly in rural areas. This software will potentially increase the involvement of renewable energy contractors to the healthcare sector and create pathways for business opportunities. This will have a direct economic impact in the long run and benefit multiple parties in the process.  The project envisions several economic benefits for Egypt and other similar countries that are striving towards green technology development. Firstly, this project aims to reduce the thermal loads in the healthcare facilities. To implement that several modifications in the existing buildings will be necessary and thus it will open business opportunities to construction companies. This project will also create business opportunities for renewable energy suppliers and installers to supply PV & battery systems to healthcare facilities. Moreover, this project will reduce the dependency on the grid energy supply which will help the grid to face less blackout during the natural gas shortage. Finally, this project will make the healthcare system more resilient and help them to operate more economically due to load reduction strategies and in-house energy production through PV.  Throughout the development of the software, there will be ongoing consultations with hospital officials and utility partners.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: A novel screening method for liver fibrosis following liver fluke infection: a new role of H. pylori
descriptions:
"Millions of inhabitants of the Lower Mekong basin region are infected with
the liver fluke, Opisthorchis viverrini (OV), that can result in liver fibrosis
(APF) and progress to cholangiocarcinoma (CCA). While infection rates in
some regions are decreasing (due to screening/treatment/education
programmes), CCA still accounts for ~10k deaths/year in Thailand alone.
We have recently shown that at 12 months follow up following praziquantel
to clear the liver fluke, ~40% of individuals have persistent or worsening
APF. Clearly, new understanding of the molecular pathology of this
disease is urgently needed to develop new, effective treatments. Recent
novel and exciting observations from our team lead us to propose that a
novel CagA+ strain of H.pylori, co-infects with OV (which is a reservoir for
this bacterial pathogen) and colonises the bile ducts to induce inflammatory
damage to cholangiocytes leading to fibrosis and CCA. We have now
characterized this novel CagA+ H.pylori from the bile of patients with CCA
(defined as biliary CagA+) and generated both recombinant protein and
antibodies: these will be used in novel assays to quantify the presence of
this pathogen in a cohort of OV-infected individuals 12 months post
treatment with praziquantel. We will monitor their liver disease by
ultrasonography and measure the presence of this novel biliary CagA+
H.pylori. We hypothesise that those with persistent or worsening fibrosis
following liver fluke clearance will have higher incidence of biliary CagA+.
The outcomes of this project will be (a) development of novel diagnostic
tools to screen those at risk of developing fibrosis following OV infection
and (b) compelling evidence supporting the role of biliary CagA+ H.pylori in
persistent liver fibrosis that will justify a clinical trial of anti-Helicobacter
therapy and hence a rapid and cost-effective route to impact."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: A machine vision-based approach for sustainable dairy farming in tropical environments
descriptions: Livestock are responsible for ~6% of greenhouse gas emissions caused by human activity, but dairy products in particular are an important source of nutrition and will continue to be critical for food security nationally and internationally where land is unsuitable for crop production. It is therefore essential to achieve sustainable dairy farming which both mitigates its high carbon footprint and is resilient to climate change. Heat stress is a critical animal welfare issue in Thailand, where high temperatures and humidity severely reduce cow comfort, milk yields, and fertility. As climate change intensifies, the problem will become important in the UK and is becoming even more urgent in Thailand, with direct consequences for food security, farmer livelihoods, and rural economies. The power of frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI) is starting to drive Precision Livestock Farming, but also illustrates the disconnect with the underpinning evidence-based research, which is still largely based on traditional research methodologies. The BBSRC-funded John Oldacre Centre for Dairy Welfare & Sustainability Research was incepted at Bristol Veterinary School in 2020 with a network of 60 cameras now monitoring the activity and behaviour of our herd of 200 cattle, linked with production and reproductive data, genetics and veterinary records to answer fundamental challenges in livestock production related to health, welfare and sustainability. This collaboration between the University of Bristol and Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok brings together UK and Thai expertise to translate this unique research platform to a tropical dairy farming context. By building Thai research capacity, we will establish a centre of excellence and resource hub for joint UK/Thailand sustainable research and innovation. We will design and implement the AI compute and storage architecture, fine-tuning the training of our jointly-developed AI methodology to realise continuous 20-camera monitoring of the 50-cow herd at Saraburi Dairy Research Farm. We will then perform the first study on the platform, aiming to identify early behavioural signs of heat stress, such as reduced feeding, changes in resting or standing patterns, or unusual social behaviour. By linking behaviour with climate conditions, we aim to develop predictive tools for heat stress events and identify the most cost-effective camera placements for farm use. This will lay the groundwork for scalable monitoring solutions that can be deployed across commercial farms in Thailand and other tropical countries. These early warnings will allow farmers to intervene quickly, improving cow welfare and productivity while preventing costly losses. The IPSF partnership will build capacity through joint training activities, strengthening Thailand’s expertise in AI and veterinary applications, directly supporting national priorities in food security, smart agriculture, and data-driven research. The impact will extend beyond academia. In the short term, dairy farmers will gain practical tools to improve herd welfare and farm efficiency. In the medium term, the approach will help strengthen the resilience of the dairy sector to climate change, contributing to national food security, rural development, and sustainable agriculture. Globally, the project demonstrates how science partnerships can create innovative solutions that benefit society, the economy, and the environment.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: An AI-Enabled Bioacoustics System for Improving the Effectiveness Fall Armyworm Traps
descriptions:
"This research aims to improve the effectiveness of pheromone-based traps
used to control the fall armyworm (FAW), by using AI-enabled bioacoustics
to identify the pest before it achieves sexual maturity. The fallarmyworm,
Spodoptera frugiperda, is an alien invasive insect in Africa, Asia and the
Pacific that feeds on more than 80 crops. However, it's prefered host crop
is maize, and in most cases millet, sorghum, and vegetable crops. The
term ""armyworm"" can refer to several species, often describing the
large-scale invasive behaviour of the species' larval stage. FAW is a global
threat to food security. In Kenya, farmers lose up to 50% of their maize,
millet and sorghum crops to the FAW, annually. The loss of these crops
has a devastating effect on rural economies, where healthy crops are often
the difference between survival and starvation. FAW reproduces and
spreads rapidly, thus early detection is key to its management.
The effectiveness of pheromone traps relies on catching male moths by
disrupting their mating behaviour, or catching female moths before they lay
their eggs on the crops. However, current trapping approaches present
many challenges including difficulty in accurately assessing pest biology
and the early onset of FAW infestation. AI-enabled bioacoustics offers an
innovative approach for detecting early age signatures of the FAW moth
that can be used to inform the placement and activation of traps. This
research will use acoustic signals produced by the FAW moth to develop
machine-learning models for identifying its early age and gender
signatures. The outcome of this research promises significant scientific,
economic and social benefits including: (1) early detection of the FAW; (2)
control measures with improved outcomes; (3) reduction in economic and
social impact of FAW outbreaks on rural communities; (4) dataset for
scientists to explore interesting FAW characteristics and inspire better
control measures"

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Investigation of an Unidentified Chayote disease in Sto. NiÃ±o Legacy Mine, Tublay, Benguet Province, Philippines
descriptions:
"Chayote (Sechium edule, Jacq. Sw, ""vegetable pear"", sayote in Filipino) is
an important economic plant and used in traditional medicine in the
Philippines. However, in recent years chayote farming has been challenged
by a disease with symptoms of fruit shrivelling with subsequent reduction of
the size of ripe fruits which regularly occurs after the second or third crop
cycle. Smaller fruits mean lower market value and income loss for farmers.
Based on previous community surveys by the project partners as part of an
on-going project on the biodiversity audit of the legacy mine in the
Barangay Sto. Niño, farmers have not found a cost effective mitigation for
the disease and regular purchase of new plants from other regions is not
economically sustainable for the community. In response to this, our
proposed project aims to identify the viral pathogen agent using a
combination of rapid detection assays and cutting edge sequencing
technologies. We will devise together with the local community mitigation
strategies to reduce occurrence and/or treatment of chayote disease. The
study will focus on Sto. Niño, Tublay, Benguet, which is a major producer
of chayote in the northern Luzon and supplier for nearby provinces
including Metro Manila. We will use an extensive existing geochemical
database from an on-going project to evaluate the relationship between soil
geochemistry and chayote disease. This new and innovative research
project will help to further develop our existing collaborations with
institutions, local governments and farming cooperatives as well as building
new institutional links. The results will plan for targeted disease
interventions for direct benefit of the community to improve the health and
sustainability of their chayote farming, and enable secured livelihood for the
future. This site specific research system will be used as a model for more
widespread implementation of chayote and other plant diseases in the
Philippines ."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Combating Urban Extreme Heat for Vulnerable Populations in Cairo
descriptions:
"Cities in low-latitudes are experiencing unequal increases in extreme heat
under diverse global-warming scenarios with the risk of reaching fatal
thresholds with minimal temperature increases [1],[2]. Additionally, the
concurrence of urban heat islands and heatwaves can amplify mortality
rates in vulnerable urban areas [3],[4]. Despite increasing awareness of the
health risks posed by heat-events, many high-density cities remain
unprepared to address these challenges due to limited understanding of
the broader public health impacts of heat. This collaboration aims to
address this gap specifically by generating new evidence and insights on
the impacts of climate change on heat-related health issues in Cairo. The
megacity experiences significant heat events, like the one in 2015, when
temperatures reaching up to 49 DegC led to substantial fatalities [5],[6].
Recent studies [7],[8],[9] demonstrate acute heat-vulnerability in most of its
urban core. Very few studies, however, explore local practices for coping
with heat-events, which our study aims to address. While some propose
potential mitigation strategies, the literature remains incomplete. Our study
will enhance the collaborative effort by examining the heat exposure of
Cairo through satellite remote-sensing data and by delving into specific
case-studies. Additionally, we will collect data on local heat-perceptions
and socio-cultural practices related to living with heat. Alongside,
microclimate-measurements will be conducted to support analysis and
identify potential localised interventions. The study extends the findings of a
previous work [10] by HK and SG that formulated design guidelines for
enhancing green/healthy spaces across deprived communities in Cairo.
Drawing on the new evidence generated, it will be possible to extend the
scope of the earlier study and collect pilot data that will support test
interventions for heat-health proofing through heat-mitigation strategies for
vulnerable communities."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Hi-IMPACTS: Hi-tech Integrated Monitoring of Pollinators for Agricultural and City Sustainability
descriptions: Pollinators provide essential ecosystem services, pollinating the large majority of plant species worldwide. However, pollinator populations are declining worldwide, affecting the reproduction of economically and ecologically important plant species. Numerous drivers are known to contribute to pollinator declines, including agricultural intensification and urbanization. Yet most knowledge on the subject has been acquired in temperate regions, and we still know very little about how tropical pollinators are affected by anthropogenic change. Moreover, strategies and frameworks developed in temperate countries may not be appropriate or effective in tropical countries. In order to protect tropical pollinators, monitoring and research are urgently needed, but traditional methods of monitoring pollinators have several disadvantages. For example, visual observation of pollinator visits to flowers requires large investments in time and manpower, tends to miss rare species, is difficult to identify pollinators on the go and difficult to catch specimens, and requires taxonomists to help identify difficult taxa. Passive insect trapping is much less time-intensive, but cannot confirm which species are true pollinators and requires trained taxonomists to help identify specimens. These shortcomings have spurred the development of novel tech-based methods such as computer vision and molecular techniques. Computer vision uses deep learning models to enable computers to obtain information from images or videos. Researchers can simply set up video cameras and then use computer vision to automatically detect which sections of the video footage contain pollinators and even identify distinct pollinator taxonomic groups. Another new tool is eDNA (environmental DNA), which are trace amounts of DNA shed by living organisms into the environment. eDNA can be isolated from environmental or biological samples (e.g., soil or flowers), amplified, and sequenced via metabarcoding for species identification. Pollinators deposit DNA on flowers during foraging, and this eDNA can be used to determine the pollinator species present in an area at high taxonomic resolution without requiring the expertise of trained taxonomists. Moreover, DNA metabarcoding of honey can provide valuable information on the foraging habits of honey bees and some elusive pollinators such as stingless bees. Our collaboration between Cranfield University (UK) and Mahidol University (Thailand) proposes to further develop these tech-based methods to improve their accuracy, efficiency, and utility in monitoring pollinators. We will also use our optimized computer vision and eDNA methodologies to examine how pollinators in central Thailand are influenced by agricultural intensification (through comparison of organic and conventional farms) and urbanization (through comparison of urban, suburban, and rural parks). The two optimized tech-based methods will be used in conjunction with traditional methods (visual observation and insect trapping) to assess their validity and effectiveness. The outputs of this collaboration will address SDGs regarding sustainable cities and agriculture and will provide both immediate and long-term benefits to Thailand and other understudied tropical areas. Namely, our outputs will inform sustainable agricultural practices that promote pollinator conservation and ensuing farmer profits (e.g., optimal floral diversity and mowing frequency), and inform city planning to support urban pollinator populations and sustainable cities (e.g., flower species attractive to native pollinators).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Targeted brain delivery Using Modern Pharmaceutical innovation of Antiepileptic drug to Solve drug-resistant Epilepsy in Indonesia (TUMPAS Epilepsy In
descriptions:
"Around 1-2 million people in Indonesia live with epilepsy– approximately 30% of these are drug-resistant. The most common type of drug-resistant epilepsy in Indonesia is focal temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). Drug-resistant epilepsy poses a significant healthcare challenge specifically in Indonesia; where there is limited access to effective medications. In other Asian countries (i.e: Taiwan or Hong Kong), drug-resistance is overcome with surgical interventions, which can be effective in seizure control. However, Indonesian cultural norms discourage surgical interventions, particularly in the brain. Drug-resistant epilepsy can result from factors that hinder delivery of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) to the brain, including the blood-brain-barrier, efflux transporters, as well as neuroinflammation. Uncontrolled epilepsy has major consequences including heightened risk of injuries, cognitive decline, and psychosocial burdens. Therefore, there is an urgent need to address the concern of drug-resistant epilepsy in Indonesia by improving treatment options.
This project aims to address aforementioned challenges through a multifaceted approach outlined in three objectives. Objective 1 focuses on developing models of drug-resistant TLE and using them to assess pharmacokinetic profile of commonly used AEDs in Indonesia. We will use internationally-validated mouse-models of TLE and develop cellular in-vitro models to study drug-cell interactions. Objective 2 involves reformulating and characterizing drug formulations of existing AEDs in Indonesia to optimize CNS uptake. The assembled group has wide-ranging formulation expertise including nanoparticles and microneedle patches. Formulations will be characterized with state-of-art instrumentations, then drug release and kinetics will be evaluated to establish optimized formulation to take progress to animal studies. Objective 3 includes testing efficacy and pharmacokinetic profile of the newly-developed AED formulations in the TLE animal model. The central goal is to discover the best AEDs and optimized formulation for TLE treatment in Indonesia, in-place of surgical interventions. This will improve clinical practices, elevate standards of patient care, and optimize healthcare resource allocation in Indonesia. This project is endorsed by Indonesian neurologists specializing in epilepsy and we will work faithfully to involve individuals affected by drug-resistant epilepsy in Indonesia to deliver an effective and sustainable healthcare approach for this challenge.
This project holds important short to medium term impact on a range of stakeholders in Indonesia. By improving understanding and management of drug resistant epilepsy, the project endeavours to directly benefit individuals affected by this condition, improving quality of life and productivity. Furthermore, increasing national conversations about epilepsy will help to improve knowledge and tackle societal stigma with epilepsy in Indonesia. Findings may then inform policy decisions aimed at improving diagnosis, and treatment, ultimately contributing to public health initiatives as well as socioeconomic development in Indonesia. By providing evidence of the best antiepileptic drug and formulation choice for use of drug-resistant epilepsy treatment in Indonesia, we hope to guide the national insurance (BPJS) in Indonesia to make an informed choice of the AED formulation that should be covered under national insurance for health. Finally, we aim to build long-standing collaborations between the epilepsy research community in the UK and Indonesia to tackle the global challenge of drug-resistant epilepsy in both countries."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Efficient Removal of Antibiotic Residues from Aqua Environment to Tackle the Antimicrobial Resistance Crisis in Turkey
descriptions:
"The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a serious threat to
global public health. According to OECD (Organisations for Economic
Cooperation and Development), Turkey took important steps to tackle
AMR, yet it remains a great risk for population health and healthcare
budget in short-medium timeframe. Among various factors contributing to
the spread of AMR, ineffective treatment of wastewaters polluted with
antibiotics constitutes to a significant proportion. Wastewater treatment
plants in Turkey lack the advanced systems needed to purify antibiotic
pollution before discharging wastewater back into the environment.
Our research project aims to develop a sustainable and scalable filtration
system able to remove multiple classes of antibiotic pollutants from
wastewaters. The research will involve the design, chemical and physical
analyses of alginate-based removal agents that is capable to remove
different antibiotic classes from water. The alginate system will be coated to
enhance its environmental stability and improve its mechanical resistance
under filtration pressure. The designed agents' removal capacity,
mechanism and kinetics toward different classes of antibiotics will be
investigated. In addition, a laboratory scale vertical filtration system will be
designed and fully validated using actual wastewater samples and
microbiological studies will be performed to confirm the full removal of
antibiotic residues and the protection of the natural microbiome.
Development of this antibiotic removal system hold the potential to
significantly reduce antibiotic contamination in water sources, thereby
mitigating the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance. By
addressing a crucial cause of AMR, this project contributes to the broader
global effort to safeguard public health and preserve the efficacy of existing
antibiotics for future generations."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Upcycling of virgin coconut oil processing by-products into coconut protein concentrates and its application in plant-based milk alternatives
descriptions:
"The anticipated growth of the Philippine virgin coconut oil (VCO)
processing industry brings with it an increasing amount of VCO processing
by-products, which to date are only partially valorised. Up to 50% of the
coconut milk mass used for VCO production is comprised of the coconut
skim milk (CSM). The main volumes of CSM are managed as waste and,
therefore, presents negative environmental concern, impacting the overall
sustainability of the VCO industry. The considerable nutrient contents of
CSM render it highly perishable and demands significant resources for
efficient waste management. The general objective of this project is to
design an upcycling strategy that will valorise CSM and reintroduce it into
the food chain in the form of protein-based ingredients. We have outlined a
UK-Philippines collaboration that will initially (I) isolate protein-rich solids
(i.e., coconut protein concentrates, CPC) from the CSM and assess its
ingredient functionality and nutrient profiles. Four additional work packages
include: II) Conversion of the CPC into protein hydrolysates (CPCH) to
address the limited solubility of CP; III) Optimisation of plant-based milk
alternative (PBMA) prototypes using CPC or CPCH in combination with
chickpea milk (a known good source of fibre and calcium); IV) Assessment
of the impact of the PBMA prototypes on human gut microbiota and
intestinal barrier function; and V) Determination of the stability and
microbiological safety of the PBMA. This collaboration brings together the
University of the Philippines Diliman (UPD) and University of Reading
(UoR) contributing complementary expertise in analytical/flavour science,
protein isolation, human gut health studies, and product development. In
addition to the exchange of knowledge and skills, this project will introduce
a whole value chain from starting raw materials to exploitable products and
technologies to our beneficiaries to maximise the use of CSM."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Expanding openScopes Africa to establish research grade open-source advanced microscopy infrastructure in Kenya and its applications in malaria diagno
descriptions:
"Recent technological advancements have expanded optical microscopy capabilities, driven by computational techniques, improved light sources, and detectors. However commercial research-grade microscopes can be expensive in resource-constrained settings, service engineers can be unavailable or prohibitively expensive, and complex proprietary instruments can become obsolete or unusable. A cost-effective and locally sustainable alternative approach is to enable (LMIC) scientists to locally assemble modular instruments from off-the-shelf or self-built components and utilize open-source software for instrument control and data analysis. Having learned to assemble and operate such instruments, local scientists can then maintain and even upgrade them to match local needs and aspirations. However, most self-built systems either use commercial microscope stands with proprietary hardware and software or require extensive specialised expertise to construct instruments from scratch using generic components that may be hard to source in Kenya. The modular openFrame-based microscopes developed as part of the openScopes programme (www.openScopes.com) by Paul French’s laboratory at Imperial College London, UK, is specifically designed to address these challenges, combining open hardware and open-source software to realise research-grade microscopes offering advanced capabilities. CAD files, software and parts lists are freely shared and openFrame-based microscopes can be assembled rapidly by users who understand the general principles of the intended instrument.
This work proposes to establish an openScopes Microscope center in Kenya. This center will be equipped to provide a range of microscopy modalities including brightfield and fluorescence imaging, with modules to upgrade the capability to super-resolution microscopy, quantitative phase imaging and photothermal microscopy, thereby facilitating cutting-edge bio-imaging research and providing world-class training opportunities. By enhancing research capabilities in Kenya and the broader East and Central African scientific community, this facility aims to significantly enhance scientific capabilities and collaboration across the continent. Additionally, affiliation with the African Biomedical Imaging Consortium (ABIC) and linking with the openScopes Africa project started at the University of Cape Town would reinforce the center’s outreach and impact across the continent, fostering a more inclusive and innovative research environment in Africa. An example of developing local research capacity would be our development of a photothermal-based module for the openFrame microscope to be explored for malaria diagnosis. This module would be based on research already undertaken in Kenya by DMM.
Malaria remains one of Africa’s most pressing health challenges. According to the 2021 World Malaria Report, there were an estimated 241 million malaria cases in 2020, 95 percent of them in Africa. An estimated 627,000 people died from malaria in 2020, mostly children under age 5. The study and diagnosis of malaria leans heavily on light microscopy, and we would hold a workshop targeting scientists in East and Central Africa to introduce and train them in the capabilities of openScopes instrumentation, including photothermal microscopy."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Clean Hydrogen and CO2 Storage for Energy Transition: From Surface Science Toward Field-Scale Implementation
descriptions:
"A grand challenge of the 21st century is to reduce society’s demand on fossil fuels and move to renewable, cleaner resources for our energy. Hydrogen is that solution, offering many benefits in terms of the environment, energy security, economic growth and energy stability. However, this switch is not immediate, but there needs to be an immediate solution to pollution resulting from fossil-based energy.

Hydrogen already serves society in many ways, being critical to make ammonia that is converted into fertilizer which is needed to promote crop yields to feed growing populations. This hydrogen comes from splitting methane (CH4) which produces carbon dioxide (CO2) that is bad for the environment. This CO2 must be captured and stored, and engineers have decided that it can be stored in subsurface reservoirs. The process of producing ‘blue’ hydrogen (due to CO2 storage) is ready, however unknowns about storage capacities and uncertainties around the integrity of storing CO2 in reservoirs remain.

Beyond CO2 storage, hydrogen can also be stored as excess energy produced from renewable resources, which can then be used when renewable generation is low, thus providing a route to stabilize energy supply. However, like CO2, there are unknowns that must be addressed before the energy transition can be realized.

This international collaboration reflects the needs to reach a solution, bringing teams of global scientists/engineers together from different disciplines to work collectively on these complex problems. The teams at Chiang Mai University and University of Leeds comprise of colloids and surface scientists, chemical engineers, petrophysicists, computational modellers, geophysicists, geoscientists and reservoir engineers, who will work across the length scales from pore-scale, through to core-scale and eventually field-scale engineering. ULEEDS brings its expertise in surface science to understand pore-scale phenomena, while CMU brings its expertise and wider network of collaborators to evaluate core- and field-scale phenomena. Only by linking the length scales, and validating computational modelling with experiments, can those uncertainties be answered.

Together with stakeholders, the project will: (i) establish a UK-Thailand centre as a focal point for bilateral activities supporting technology and innovation transfer by means of research facilities sharing and workshops; (ii) develop early-career researchers in a critical area; and (iii) undertake fundamental-to-engineering research delivering high quality publications and/or intellectual property.

In addition to capacity building, the short-term impact will focus on technology and innovation transfer to Thai researchers and industrialists in energy and hard-to-abate industries, and ecosystems on CCS and hydrogen energy, especially those energy-related industries (National consortia on hydrogen energy and renewables, and National Committee on Climate Change).

The mid-term impact will be to deliver tangible knowledge on georesources potential for CGS and UHS, in support of national policies on energy and climate (e.g., scientific-based policy). Policy makers will be lobbied in the Departments of Mineral Fuels and Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand of Ministry of Energy, and Mineral Resources of Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment.

Outcomes of the project will be publicly shared to build acceptance of subsurface storage for the energy transition."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Optimization of subcutaneous transplantation of mesenchymal stem cell-derived insulin producing cells for the treatment of diabetes mellitus.
descriptions: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a metabolic disease that is a major health concern and among the top ten causes of deaths worldwide, places a significant demand on healthcare systems. Moreover, DM is a common complication of kidney transplantation. It results from a deficiency of insulin production in T1DM or an inability to utilize this hormone as in T2DM. In Egypt, ~11 million had diabetes and this number is expected to rise to 13 million by 2030 and to 20 million by 2045, making Egypt 10th among countries with highest prevalence of DM by 2045. We implemented pre-clinical trials on our laboratory with nude mice based on utilizing mesenchymal stem cells, which demonstrated effective treatment for diabetes post transplantation of insulin producing cells derived from mesenchymal stem cells under the renal capsule, but this surgical procedure is invasive.
