The subcutaneous space is the least invasive, possess a wide space, and it allows monitoring of the grafted cells. However, subcutaneous space’s primary limitation is its poor vascularization. To mitigate this issue, scaffolds can be used due to their ability to release oxygen and nutrients or to enhance neovascularization. Our initial studies with scaffolds (1-layer) produced by the Prof Lamprou Team at QUB and tested by the Egyptian team in Sprague Dawley rats, have shown that tissues adjacent to the transplanted scaffolds revealed enhanced vascularization as compared to the control sample, and have also provide higher cell acceptance by any other commercial scaffolds. However, these cells will not be able to survive for longer times; therefore, a multilayer scaffold will need to be manufactured. A microvascular network is required to facilitate tissue ingrowth into any scaffold. The proposal aims to prepare by 3D bioprinting a multilayer scaffold (3-layers), with each layer have different properties that needed for the current application and keeping the cells alive and active.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Transforming Crop Breeding: Building Tomorrow’s Talent through UK–Thailand Collaboration in Integrated Breeding and Genome Editing for Resilient Agric
descriptions:
This proposal directly addresses Thailand’s national development challenges by advancing food security, climate resilience and equitable access to agricultural innovation. Although Thailand is classified as an upper middle-income country, nearly one third of its population remains employed in agriculture, with rural communities – particularly smallholder farmers – vulnerable to climatic shocks, soil degradation and market volatility. These populations operate with limited access to improved crop varieties and technological innovation, leading to persistent disparities in productivity, income and adaptive capacity. 
The national breeding system faces two primary bottlenecks: (1) a heavy reliance on conventional breeding methods, which are slow and insufficient for addressing emerging environmental and economic challenges; and (2)limited integration of modern molecular tools including genome editing into public sector breeding pipelines. These limitations restrict the timely delivery of climate resilient and market relevant varieties to smallholders, particularly for critical crops such as cassava, maize and sugarcane, which underpin both subsistence and commercial farming livelihoods.
This project provides a targeted, scalable response. It builds Thai institutional and human capacity in genomics integrated and precision breeding by embedding advanced functional genomics, genome editing and quantitative trait analysis into KU-led training and field activities. Co-designed with Thai institutions and stakeholders, the project ensures that new methods directly address national breeding goals while being locally owned and contextually appropriate.
Within a ten-year timeframe, this collaboration will deliver tangible, measurable outcomes that benefit low income and vulnerable communities. These include:
-Faster varietal development cycles for climate resilient crops, improving yield stability under heat, drought and shifting growing seasons
-Improved access to modern seed for smallholders through strengthened links between public breeders, seed companies and farmer networks
-Reduced breeding costs and dependency on imported germplasm by embedding low cost, locally managed genomic methods into Thai breeding stations
-Increased inclusion of women and early career scientists, addressing the skills gap and generational divide in Thailand’s agri-research sector
-Broader public and private translation of research, connecting innovation outputs with farmer ready delivery channels
By co-developing toolkits, digital learning platforms and genome editing policy trackers, the project also supports long-term regulatory readiness and ecosystem development. It complements Thailand’s Bioeconomy Roadmap and National Biotechnology Policy by offering practical implementation pathways that strengthen delivery systems at both national and community levels.
Crucially, the project avoids extractive models of collaboration.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of biocontrol agents to overcome papaya dieback disease in Malaysia
descriptions:
"Papaya is one of the major tropical fruits grown worldwide, and Malaysia is
the primary exporter of it in Asia. The production of papaya in Malaysia was
reduced by up to 70% due to the recent spread of papaya dieback disease,
which led to the loss of US$58 million with its initial outbreak alone. A
treatment for papaya dieback is urgently needed to prevent crop losses.
Biological control makes use of beneficial microbes to kill those that cause
disease and is one potential solution to treat papaya dieback. In our
previous work, we have isolated beneficial microbes that inhibit the growth
of the papaya dieback pathogen. The aim of the present application is to
assess the suitability of two selected microbes, one bacterial and one
fungal strain, to be used to contain papaya dieback disease. We will
determine how the papaya plants respond to the treatment with the two
biocontrol strains, as well as how effective these are in preventing the
development of the disease. We will also study the antimicrobial
metabolites produced by the biocontrol strains using a combination of
genomics and metabolomics. The goal of this work is to develop spray
formulations in collaboration with our industrial partner, Bumi Alam Lestari,
that can be used for the sustainable biological control of papaya dieback
disease by farmers in Malaysia. The proposed research will have strong
scientific and economic long term impact. It will aid farmers in Malaysia in
the cultivation of one of their major crops. It will lead to improving crop
yields, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals of Zero Hunger,
Responsible Consumption and Production, and Life on Land, as well as
with the ISPF theme of Healthy People, Animals and Plants. The Malaysian
economy will benefit from the proposed activity as it will lead to reduced
crop losses. The scientific community will also benefit, as we will train
early-career researchers in Malaysia on the development of biocontrol
agents for crop protection."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: From waste to wellness: Valorizing food by-products to generate health promoting plant extracts targeting gut metabolism.
descriptions: It is well established that the gut microbiota plays a central role in shaping human health and maintaining well-being, and that the gut microbiome can be manipulated by targeted dietary interventions. Valorization of food by-products is a pivotal strategy in sustainable food production and waste management. Interestingly, food byproducts represent a copious reservoir of bioactive compounds that can beneficially alter the gut microbiome and can be retrieved via innovative extraction and processing techniques to unlock their nutritional and economic potential. This collaborative project links relevant expertise and capabilities at QIB (UK) and Ain Shams University (Egypt) and seeks to identify food byproduct sources of phytochemicals that can beneficially affect the human gut microbiota and develop sustainable extraction protocols to generate novel ingredients targeting gut (and host) health. The main target will be gut microbial metabolism; effects of extracts on the gut microbiome will be assessed using various in vitro human colon models at QIB, and biotransformation of the polyphenols by the microbiota will also be assessed by combining shotgun metagenomics analysis with metabolome data, hence relationships between the gut microbiome and metabolite changes will be explored. The overall approach will be to identify suitable byproducts and generate extracts (led by ASU), assess their potential to beneficially alter microbial metabolism (QIB) and to generate protocols for efficient extraction and final product preparation. This collaborative project will address several sustainable development goals; valorizing food by-products, reducing food waste, ensuring more efficient use of resources. Besides, the project would pave the way to collaboration with food industry partners for the formulation of products derived from the optimized extracts for promoting human health.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Recentrailsation reform in Vietnam: an analysis of its effects on economic activity and corruption
descriptions:
"The ""age of decentralisation"" saw many countries devolve government
power to subnational units. The aim was to enhance local democracy,
public service delivery, and accountability. However, decentralisation often
fell short of expectations, leading to recentralisation trends.
Recentralisation aims to address issues like bureaucratic inefficiency and
local elite capture. Despite its significance, the economic impact of
recentralisation remains understudied. This research aims to fill this gap by
analysing how recentralisation affects economic drivers. Competing
theories suggest recentralisation may boost investment by streamlining
institutions and reducing duplication, or hinder investment by disconnecting
from local firms and weakening political ties.
We will investigate the impact of a recent pilot program of government
recentralisation, which took place in 10 of the 63 provinces of Vietnam
during 2009-2015, on various aspects of local economic activity, ranging
from corporate investment, employment, and production, to corruption and
the efficiency of public administration. Utilising data from public surveys, we
will employ advanced event-study and Difference in Differences (DiD)
techniques to compare evidence from the reform period with periods before
and after.
The collaboration will provide the VNU partner team both on-the-job and
formal training in advanced data analysis for policy making, including a
week-long workshop on advanced DiD and panel-data techniques by the
associate partner. Additionally, the collaboration aims to introduce a wider
audience of government officials and scholars in Vietnam to
evidence-based economic policy analysis, and to establish a network of
connections in Vietnam for the continued involvement of the three partners
in providing economic policy advice using empirical analysis and
applications of theoretical reasoning and intuition."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Scaling Up High-Performance Hybrid Microbial Fuel Cells for Sustainable Energy Recovery from Petroleum Wastewater: A Pilot-Scale Demonstration
descriptions:
"The escalating global demand for energy and the increasing generation of hazardous cutting fluid wastewater from manufacturing processes like milling and turning necessitate the development of sustainable and innovative treatment solutions. This pilot-scale study proposes a groundbreaking approach to address these interconnected challenges by scaling up high-performance hybrid microbial fuel cells (MFCs) for concurrent energy recovery and wastewater remediation.

Central to this innovation is the discovery and utilization of novel electroactive microorganisms with the rare and sought-after capability to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons, a major component of cutting fluids, while generating an electrical current. This biological process offers a chemical-free, sustainable alternative to conventional wastewater treatment methods.

To enhance energy output, we will investigate roughened electrode materials, providing increased surface area for microbial attachment and electron transfer. The electricity generated will be harvested and stored in supercapacitors, powering a network of low-current sensors for real-time monitoring and optimization of the treatment process.

A pilot-scale MFC system will be deployed directly at a manufacturing facility, showcasing its real-world applicability and scalability in treating cutting fluid wastewater. We anticipate a significant reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) from 33.16 g/L to less than 5 g/L and fats, oils, and grease (FOG) from 2500 mg/L to less than 400 mg/L within 4 days of treatment, highlighting the efficacy of this microbial-driven remediation approach. Rigorous data collection and analysis will evaluate energy recovery efficiency, wastewater treatment efficacy, and potential for upscaling to larger industrial applications.

This research has the potential to revolutionize wastewater treatment in the manufacturing industry. By harnessing the unique capabilities of petroleum-degrading electroactive microorganisms and integrating them with advanced energy storage and sensor technologies, we aim to develop a scalable, sustainable, and cost-effective solution for both energy generation and environmental remediation. The successful implementation of this technology could significantly reduce the industry’s reliance on fossil fuels, while simultaneously mitigating the environmental impact of its waste streams. This aligns with the global push towards a circular economy and contributes to a cleaner and more resilient energy future."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: TRAPCAT: TRansformative Artificial Intelligence Research for Personalised CAncer Treatment
descriptions:
Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women worldwide, accounting for 25% of all women cancer. It remains a major cause of death among women globally, particularly in low/mid-income countries. GLOBOCAN’s statistics estimated 2.3 million new cases of breast cancer and 685,000 deaths worldwide in 2020.

Breast cancer **treatment can be made more effective, and personalised, by tailoring it to the individual patient’s clinical profile**. Analysis of the tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) of biomarkers such as CD3, 4 & 8, is useful in evaluating the immune microenvironment of cancer patients, and promising predictive biomarkers, for personalised treatment plans. However, each biomarker currently requires specialised immunohistochemistry (IHC) stains, and additional tissue slice per stain that are costly and time consuming. 

Virtual staining, using AI, is a new technology that has potential to **revolutionise clinical decision-making process** for breast cancer treatment as it will enable the phenotype of cells in the tumour to be predicted with accuracy based on the H&E appearances alone. In other words, it allows for visualisation of specific biomarkers, without physical staining. This is particularly useful where limited tissue samples are available, which is a common problem in practice. Virtual staining also has potential to **reduce cost and time** required for histopathology testing, which can **improve overall efficiency** in the diagnostic process, and helps the environment through reduced chemical use. This **enables and accelerates research, guides treatment decisions** and ultimately **improve patient outcomes**.

The success of this endeavour relies on availability and access to sufficient aligned and **annotated Data** (Histopathological images, and associated clinical and meta-data) as well as an **international multi-disciplinary** (clinical, computing, NGO, patient-facing) team to collaboratively address the problem. **_This project serves as a seed for cultivating future long-term collaboration & impact._**

Within this project, and to maximise the visual information available to the algorithm, we will be training the algorithm on excision specimens which have greater surface area of the tumour available for assessment, better representing the immune infiltrates. The future direction, which will follow on from this study, will be to adapt the algorithm to also work on core biopsies, and then to apply the algorithm in the neoadjuvant setting to aid in the stratification of patients for neoadjuvant treatment. It is anticipated that, as a secondary outcome to being able to predict the phenotype of the immune infiltrate, this algorithm will also predict patient outcomes. Outcome data will be available on all of the samples included in this study.
